#9880. FreshRSS API passwords create a second access path

A FreshRSS user may log in to the web interface while native apps use a separate API password. The two paths can have different exposure and logging behavior. Treating the API password as a copy of the web password obscures that boundary.

FreshRSS documents API access for mobile and native clients through the Google Reader API and the Fever API [1]. The mobile access guide instructs administrators to enable API access and users to set an API password in their profile [2]. The project's access-control documentation also describes form authentication, HTTP authentication, and an uncontrolled state with no authentication [3]. The deployment must choose one of those models deliberately.

On 2026-11-07, a ZoomEye count-only probe with title="FreshRSS", sub_type=all, page 1, and pagesize 1 returned 11,840 matches [4]. The app probe returned 9,530 and the body query 26,651. These fields can surface valid installations and product references, but they do not prove that API access is enabled or that a password is weak.

Review API enablement, per-user API passwords, OpenID Connect or HTTP authentication, and any anonymous mode. A shared deployment should not allow one user's feed list, labels, or credentials to influence another user's session. Test a user who is disabled in the web interface but still has an API password, and a password change that does not invalidate an existing client.

FreshRSS stores feed endpoints and may hold credentials or tokens used to fetch private sources. Those values belong to the same trust boundary as the user's session. Restrict server egress to expected destinations, separate administrative access from user accounts, and avoid placing API passwords in URLs or public dashboards. If a feed URL contains a secret, rotate it when the feed is changed.

Use TLS, a supported authentication mode, and a reverse proxy that does not bypass the API path. Review the documented web-server instructions for protecting the API separately from the main interface [3]. Back up user and feed metadata with encryption and test restoration. Monitor repeated authentication failures and unusual feed additions.

A ZoomEye title query can identify a product page for an authorized inventory check. It cannot show whether the instance is a test server, whether anonymous access is enabled, or whether a user has an API password. Confirm ownership and use approved configuration access before drawing an exposure conclusion.

FreshRSS connects users to external feeds and stores their reading state. The separate API path deserves its own lifecycle and test coverage.

#9879. “Move Fast and Break Things” Is Dead. What Counts in Enterprise AI Now?

The AI-Native CEO podcast host and newsletter author, AI automation specialist, and communications executive.

The AI-Native CEO podcast host and newsletter author, AI automation specialist, and communications executive.

The AI-Native CEO podcast host and newsletter author, AI automation specialist, and communications executive.

The invoices are ending Silicon Valley’s favorite motto that built the AI boom.

Right before Facebook went public, Mark Zuckerberg shared the “move fast and break things” motto in his 2012 letter to investors. The idea was to build and launch quickly, fix problems later, and learn from mistakes. Startups across Silicon Valley embraced this approach. During the web and mobile boom, the focus was on gaining users first, with monetization, compliance, and governance left for later. When ChatGPT entered the market, the industry repeated this strategy on a larger scale. Companies scrambled for computing power and began spending heavily on licenses, pilots, and APIs, treating AI as a land grab.

At Facebook’s developer conference in April 2014, Zuckerberg joked about a new motto: “move fast with stable infra.” With 1.28 billion users, breaking things had become expensive.

The motto worked until mistakes became more expensive because of the token costs, and the results stopped matching expectations. In a PwC survey of 4,454 CEOs, 56% said they had seen no significant financial benefit from AI so far.

Costs have also been harder to predict than anyone planned. A Harness study found that 72% of organizations had had an unexpected AI cost spike, and more than half said no one clearly owns AI spending. Harness sells AI cost-management software, so it has a stake in how big the problem looks. Cloudera’s research points to another problem: segmented data systems and silos make it hard for companies to measure what AI really costs them to run.

In April, Uber’s CTO Praveen Neppalli Naga said the company had used up its entire 2026 AI budget after just four months of Claude Code. Teams had been ranked on an internal leaderboard by how much AI they used. By June, the company limited each employee to $1,500 a month per AI coding tool. In August, Naga wrote that Uber was coming to the end of the so-called “tokenmaxxing era,” when burning tokens meant productivity.

Gartner's advice to CFOs is to treat AI cost as an architecture issue rather than a budget line item. One unmonitored prompt library alone can "risk running up millions of dollars in additional expense".

That’s the new rule. Finance asks the question nobody asked loudly in 2023: what did we get?

Finance teams can't parse a transformer model, but they can easily understand a unit price. Unit price is now the driver of architecture decisions. So how do you deal with that?

Route tasks wisely. Don’t just send every job to the largest model. In his annual letter on October 21, 2026, Satya Nadella introduced the “cost-to-outcome” frontier: “After all, Super Intelligence is changing every organization’s inputs (how they work) as well as their outputs (the products and services they sell). At the same time, inference is making marginal cost an important factor in software economics as usage scales. As a result, customers will increasingly measure the cost of tokens against the outcomes they produce. We call this the “cost-to-outcome” frontier, and we are focused on optimizing it.”

For engineers, that means sending classification, extraction, and summarisation to a smaller, cheaper model, caching repeated prompts, and using the frontier model only for the work that needs it.

Count everything. FinOps for AI is the top priority in the State of FinOps 2026 Report, and AI expense management is a skill teams currently need to build. In practice, that means tagging every model call by team and feature and giving each agent its own budget and alert, so a runaway loop triggers an alarm before it reaches the invoice.

A new software market is emerging to meet this demand. Max Gontar, CEO of the AI-powered finance software company Kairos, explains:

The first wave of enterprise AI was all about wild spending on experiments in the hope of seeing what the models could write/generate. The current state is that CFOs are getting what they actually need: software that runs within their existing infrastructure to find working capital leaks, deliver tangible ROI and automate finance workflows as a result (that's where AI really is good at). The new challenge for the CFO is the management of AI infrastructure spend. They now have to work out how many tokens it makes sense to spend on each process, what to cut and what to rebuild. The ROI of every function in the business will be more transparent than it's ever been.

Watch who owns the numbers. In the FinOps Foundation’s 2026 survey of 1,192 practitioners, 78% of FinOps teams report to the CTO or CIO, and only 8% report to the CFO. So finance didn’t take control, but it did get veto power. The CFO asks, “What did this return?” and engineering manages the dashboard with the answer.

There’s a problem, though. If every task has to meet a cost limit, who pays for work you can’t predict? Cost-to-serve metrics reward what’s measurable now, but exploration usually isn’t measurable in the short term.

There's no 2026 data at all to show that cost discipline is in any way reducing the amount of exploratory research so it's a valid concern rather than a fact. The moral guidelines, the risk frameworks, the ethical manifestos all sit in a PDF somewhere and are presumably being read. A runaway agent loop doesn't do that. It shows up as a number on a bill and numbers get attention. The ledger will only protect what it can count.

Here's the obvious objection: if the era is over why are the giants still throwing money at it? Forbes has the four biggest spenders (Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Alphabet) at $700-$725bn of capital expenditure in 2026, up 75% on $410bn in 2025.

This only makes the argument clearer. The sellers are the hyperscalers. They build capacity and fund it with huge cash flows, betting on future demand. Their customers are the buyers, and buyers pay attention to invoices. If a buyer cuts back, chooses cheaper models, or limits usage, it affects the demand that sellers are counting on.

There's a bit of a tension there. Capacity is being built on the basis that the enterprises will be spending a lot more, whilst the same enterprises are in fact capping their usage, moving to cheaper models and asking what they got for the money. One side of that equation is either completely wrong or just way ahead of its time.

Facebook abandoned 'move fast and break things' when it started to get expensive. A decade on and enterprise AI is running into the same wall, just with a much bigger bill. It's not over yet. Finance has the veto, they just can't yet see what they're giving up in terms of accuracy and ambition. 'Move fast and break things' died because of the invoices. The next battle is over what gets counted.

#9877. Tidal Loom: let your breathing draw a ribbon of ink

This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge.

Tidal Loom turns natural chest movement into layered ribbons of ink.

Choose terracotta, sage or ocean, sit comfortably, and let a small canvas respond to you. There is no target breathing rate, score or assessment. The interaction is simply movement becoming a mark.

A labelled illustration mode lets anyone explore the artwork before choosing camera processing. Live mode uses SmartSpectra’s chest-breathing trace. An artwork-only recorder can export a short video without including camera images or audio.

Watch the 51-second live SmartSpectra demonstration. Natural chest movement controls the ribbons; the recording includes only the artwork and its live signal label.

Try the illustration in your browser. No account or camera is needed for that mode. To run it locally, clone the repository, run node preview.mjs and open http://127.0.0.1:52106.

For live mode, follow the README’s desktop setup: npm ci, npm run build:live, then npm run start:live. Use your own SmartSpectra API key, read the data notice, give consent and choose Start with my camera. The app does not require its own account. Place your face and upper chest in view, under steady lighting, and breathe naturally.

The app uses Electron, Canvas 2D and SmartSpectra 3.4.0. Eight automated tests cover the signal’s validation/freshness gates and the sensor lifecycle, including stopping while camera permission is still pending.

The SDK requests MetricType.CHEST_BREATHING. The app decodes breathing.upperTrace, normalizes a short rolling window and smooths the resulting value. That value changes the ribbons’ amplitude, making the composition open and narrow with chest movement.

When validation fails or the data becomes stale, live animation pauses. It requires fresh valid samples to resume. Late callbacks from an ended session are ignored. Synthetic illustration mode stays explicitly labelled, including in exported footage.

Most Creative or Delightful Use of Human Signals. Tidal Loom uses the signal as an art material: a direct, visible interaction without turning it into a performance target.

Camera mode is for adults aged 18 or older and requires an explicit consent checkbox and Start. Stop clears the local motion window and ends capture. Hiding or closing the app also ends capture.

Camera images remain on the device. Tidal Loom holds at most 180 movement samples in memory and does not maintain an application database or add analytics.

Presage describes retaining Insights while the developer account is active and normally deleting them within 60 days after account closure; other records have separate retention periods. Stopping the app clears local samples, not server records. The linked SDK policy explains deletion requests and the full retention schedule.

Recording is optional. It captures only the artwork and signal-source label, with no camera frames, audio or API key. The video stays in memory until replaced or the app closes, unless explicitly downloaded. The recorder uploads nothing; downloaded files can be deleted locally.

#9876. SRT is not WebVTT: shipping a subtitle converter in a 1.17 MB player

I'm the developer of RKMovies, an ultra-lightweight 4K media player client for Android and Windows (1.17 MB APK, 29.5 MB PC installer). This is a dev diary about the part nobody blogs about: subtitles.

The upstream sources serve a mix of .srt and .vtt files. SRT uses comma decimal separators in timestamps (00:00:01,500 --> 00:00:03,200), WebVTT requires dots. The player library only speaks VTT, so every caption track goes through a converter before it reaches the renderer.

captionVtt() fetches the track text. If it already starts with WEBVTT, it passes the header through but still cleans each cue line. Otherwise it parses SRT blocks: split on blank lines, drop the numeric index line, keep the block only if the timing line contains -->, convert commas to dots, and prefix the output with WEBVTT.

The cleaning half is cleanSubtitleText(). It strips SSA/ASS override tags like {\an8}, removes HTML-ish markup (, , ), decodes entities (&,  , '), and turns
into real newlines. Most "broken subtitle" reports we got early on were just leftover markup tags rendering as literal text on screen.

For local files (.srt, .vtt, .ass uploads), fileToVtt() runs the same SRT parser over the file contents, so a downloaded subtitle file works with zero server round-trips.

On the render side I hook subtitleBeforeUpdate plus a MutationObserver on the .art-subtitle-line elements to re-clean whatever the library injects into the DOM. Font size, bottom offset and color are driven through CSS variables (--art-subtitle-font-size, --art-subtitle-bottom, --art-subtitle-color) that get recomputed on resize and orientation change, because subtitles on a 6-inch phone held at arm's length need to be bigger than on a TV.

Total cost: about 80 lines of JavaScript. Which is the point. In a player this small, features don't cost APK size, dependencies do. Subtitles in Hindi, Tamil, Telugu and English ship in the box, and the desktop app for the TV runs the same pipeline.

If you want to poke at it: the Android APK is 1.17 MB with MediaCodec hardware decode, and there is no account and no telemetry.

#9874. Google's 2027 LSA Expansion Has an API Availability Problem

Mayur Shah writes about Google Local Services Ads and review strategies for service businesses.

Mayur Shah writes about Google Local Services Ads and review strategies for service businesses.

Mayur Shah writes about Google Local Services Ads and review strategies for service businesses.

Google's planned 2027 expansion of Local Services Ads (LSAs) creates an important technical question for agencies and software providers: will Google Ads API capabilities expand at the same pace as the advertiser migration?

Google's migration roadmap says non-US accounts and remaining business categories will transition to Performance Max campaigns with pay-per-lead goals in 2027. Yet the current Google Ads API documentation still restricts the country_code field for these campaigns to US.

This is not proof that international API support will arrive late. Google may update its API documentation and regional capabilities before the relevant migration phases begin. But it exposes an integration risk that agencies should address before international accounts move into the new campaign architecture.

The issue is bigger than campaign creation. It affects account provisioning, location validation, campaign automation, conversion-goal configuration, reporting, and the ability to manage multiple markets through a single software layer.

Google is moving LSAs into a specialized Performance Max campaign structure while retaining the pay-per-lead model and local placements on Search and Maps.

Its published migration schedule has three broad phases:

August 2026: selected US home and storefront services

Late 2026: broader advertiser groups, including service-area businesses and professional services

2027: non-US accounts and remaining supported categories

The API documentation describes a more limited geographic capability at present. The Performance Max for pay-per-lead setup requires a two-letter country code in local_services_pmax_campaign_settings.country_code, and the documented supported value is US. The documentation also states that location criteria must belong to the campaign's home country.

That creates a distinction between two forms of availability:

These capabilities are related, but they are not interchangeable. A campaign becoming available in the Google Ads interface does not automatically establish that every API workflow, field, validation rule, or regional dependency is available too.

Sources: Google Ads API: Performance Max for pay-per-lead goals and supported business verticals.

Consider an agency managing campaigns for plumbing businesses in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia.

A conventional campaign-management platform might represent each account using a shared configuration:

This is a simplified internal representation, not a Google API request.

The problem emerges when the provisioning service translates that configuration into Google's campaign resource. If the API validates the country code against the currently supported value of US, an international campaign cannot simply be created by substituting GB or AU.

The integration must distinguish between a market supported by the advertising product and one supported by the API provisioning workflow.

A robust system should therefore maintain a capability registry rather than assuming that every market supports every operation.

The values above are illustrative. They should be populated from verified Google documentation and account-level eligibility checks, not treated as Google's published UK capability status.

This registry becomes particularly important during phased rollouts. Different accounts may become eligible at different times, even when they operate in the same country or vertical.

Google's API implementation has also evolved across versions.

The Local Services campaign documentation distinguishes standalone campaigns using:

from Local Services campaigns represented as specialized Performance Max campaigns:

This distinction matters for integrations that identify campaigns by advertising channel type alone.

This is part of a broader API transition problem in Google's LSA migration. As I discussed in The Hidden API Problem in Google's LSA-to-PMax Migration, changes to campaign architecture can create compatibility challenges for agencies that depend on programmatic account management. The 2027 international expansion adds another dimension: regional API availability.

Google's documentation now describes Local Services Performance Max campaign creation and management through the API starting in version v26. Earlier API versions had more limited support, including update-only workflows for eligible campaigns created through the Google Ads interface.

However, API version support and geographic eligibility are separate constraints. Supporting the required resource fields in v26 does not mean every country can use them.

An integration can therefore pass its API-version checks and still fail during campaign creation because a required country, listing, location asset, or account prerequisite is unsupported.

Source: Google Ads API: Local Services campaigns.

Local Services Performance Max campaigns are not configured independently of business-location data.

The API workflow requires a Google Business Profile listing ID through local_services_pmax_campaign_settings.listing_id. Google validates this listing during campaign creation against the associated location assets.

An international rollout may require more than accepting a new country code. It may also require market-specific validation rules, supported location criteria, phone-number formats, language constraints, and business-verification workflows.

For agencies, this means a campaign provisioning system should not treat a Google Business Profile listing ID as a globally interchangeable identifier. It must validate the relationship between the listing, the account, the market, and the campaign before submitting a mutation request.

Local Services Performance Max campaigns use a constrained set of lead conversion categories.

The current API documentation identifies:

For non-coupon campaigns, phone-call leads are automatically configured as the required active goal. Message leads are created but disabled by default. Booking goals depend on an approved Reserve with Google partner being detected on the linked location.

These rules matter because an agency cannot safely assume that a campaign's conversion configuration is identical across every market or account.

A provisioning service should validate the goals returned by the API rather than assuming that a successful campaign creation request means every intended lead channel is active.

It should also separate campaign configuration from actual lead availability. A goal being technically configurable does not guarantee that the underlying service or partner integration is available in a particular market.

Source: Google's pay-per-lead API documentation.

The practical response is to make campaign automation capability-aware.

A single global provisioning workflow is attractive, but it can become fragile when product eligibility, API support, and verification requirements change independently.

A more resilient architecture should include five components:

Maintain a market-level record of supported campaign operations, API versions, verticals, conversion goals, and location requirements. Store the source and date of each capability check.

Before creating a campaign, validate the account's market, business category, Google Business Profile listing, location assets, and required lead goals. Reject unsupported combinations before sending a mutation request.

Keep Google API resource mapping separate from internal campaign models. This makes it easier to handle changes to resource fields, validation rules, and API versions without rewriting the entire agency platform.

Use an internal provisioning state machine to prevent duplicate campaign creation when requests time out or return ambiguous errors. Record the Google resource name and mutation result before retrying.

Track API errors by country, API version, operation, campaign type, and error code. A rise in INVALID_LOCAL_SERVICES_PERFORMANCE_MAX_LISTING_ID errors, for example, should be investigated separately from country-code validation failures.

These controls also make it easier to identify whether a failure comes from account eligibility, API capability, location configuration, or a temporary service issue.

Google's 2027 LSA expansion is a significant platform change, but the most important engineering challenge may be hidden from advertisers. Agencies that depend on API-driven reporting, campaign provisioning, and multi-market automation need to prepare for regional capability differences.

The current documentation establishes a clear constraint: the documented pay-per-lead API workflow is US-specific, while Google's migration roadmap schedules non-US accounts for 2027. Whether those capabilities converge before international migration begins remains something agencies must monitor.

The safest approach is not to build international automation around an assumed rollout date. It is to build systems that can detect regional capabilities, validate account eligibility, and adapt when Google releases new API support.

A global advertising product needs more than a global migration announcement. It needs a globally consistent and documented integration surface.

#9873. How Companies Stay Online During AWS us-east-1 Outages: What the Teams That Stayed Up Did Differently

Posted on Nov 6 • Originally published at controlplane.com • AI-assisted

Companies that stayed online during AWS us-east-1 outages already ran their critical services in a second region or a second cloud, moved traffic with a small, rehearsed step or automated health-checked routing, and kept us-east-1-only services out of their failover path. Multi-AZ inside us-east-1 was not enough, because the October 2025 outage hit regional services that every availability zone depends on. On Control Plane, a platform that runs each workload active-active across regions and clouds, customers with us-east-1 in their deployment had workloads active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds during that outage, according to Control Plane’s internal incident telemetry.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

According to AWS’s post-event summary, a race condition in DynamoDB’s automated DNS management left an empty DNS record for the regional endpoint, dynamodb.us-east-1.amazonaws.com, starting at 11:48 PM PDT on October 19, 2025. DynamoDB recovered in the early hours of October 20. EC2 instance launches stayed impaired and Network Load Balancer health checks failed into the afternoon, which affected Lambda, ECS, EKS, Fargate, STS, and other services that depend on them. AWS reported full recovery at 2:20 PM PDT on October 20.

Control Plane’s Cloud Outage Tracker covers 62 major AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Cloudflare outages since 2020. Recent us-east-1 events in the tracker include:

The tracker lists 9 of AWS’s 14 major outages in us-east-1. The median major outage across all providers lasted 6h 08m.

AWS does not publish incident rates by region, so there is no official comparison of how often us-east-1 fails against other regions. Three facts are documented. us-east-1 is AWS’s oldest region, launched in 2006, and many production workloads run there. The control planes for several global AWS services run there. In the Cloud Outage Tracker, 9 of AWS’s 14 major outages since 2020 were in us-east-1, a count that is not adjusted for region size.

The control plane dependencies explain most of the spread. According to AWS’s fault isolation guidance for global services, the control planes for IAM, Route 53, CloudFront, AWS Certificate Manager certificates for CloudFront, AWS Organizations, and AWS WAF for CloudFront run in us-east-1. During a us-east-1 event, creating an IAM role, changing a Route 53 record through the API, or issuing a CloudFront certificate can fail even for workloads in other regions. Since December 2025, Route 53 offers a standby control plane endpoint in us-west-2 for updating public records during a us-east-1 event, if you configure and use it.

Data plane operations usually keep working. Route 53 DNS answers are served from AWS’s global edge network, and Route 53 health checks run in the data plane. Requests signed with existing IAM credentials are authorized by IAM’s regional data plane, though AWS reported STS and IAM sign-in errors in us-east-1 during the October 2025 event. Applications that refresh credentials through the global STS endpoint depend on us-east-1, so configure regional STS endpoints. A failover procedure that needs a us-east-1 control plane call may fail during the outage it is meant to handle.

Four engineering teams published accounts of the October 2025 outage. Each row below uses only facts from that team’s own post, plus Control Plane’s incident data.

Temporal and FireHydrant. A rehearsed failover is a short, predictable step. FireHydrant had replicated its Namespaces to a second region and tested the move in a game day, so when errors appeared it triggered the failover and its workflows kept running. Temporal’s account also shows the risk of hidden dependencies: a few auto-failovers were delayed because the failover workflow itself depended on the source region.

LoginRadius. Identity is a dependency for every other service a customer runs. LoginRadius kept its customer-facing APIs online by running stateless services in independent regions with routing at two layers.

Block. Regional diversity paid off where it existed. Cash App ran in us-west-2 and was mostly unaffected, and Square’s automated failover redirected all traffic within a half hour. European seller transactions, whose primary path ran through us-east-1, still saw up to 30% of transactions fail at peak. Block’s own lesson is that support systems such as phone support need the same redundancy as core services.

Ably. A nearby, already-running second region kept a latency-sensitive service healthy. Ably needed only a DNS change to send new connections to us-east-2, at a worst-case cost of 12 ms at p50, while existing connections in us-east-1 stayed up. Ably moved because it could not add capacity in us-east-1 as traffic grew.

The published accounts, plus AWS’s own resilience guidance, point to a common set of practices.

Availability zones protect against data center failures, power events, and localized network issues within a region. AWS designs each zone as an independent failure domain with separate power, cooling, and networking. Multi-AZ handles zone failures such as the May 7-8, 2026 single-zone event in the tracker.

A regional service is shared by every zone in the region. When the DynamoDB endpoint’s DNS record was emptied on October 19-20, 2025, services in every zone lost DynamoDB. EC2 instance launches and Network Load Balancer health checks were impaired across the region, so multi-AZ Auto Scaling groups could not reliably replace capacity. That event was regional and lasted 14h 32m. Surviving a regional failure requires a second region.

For a deeper walkthrough, see how to keep your app online when an AWS region goes down and how to test failover without taking production down.

Cell-based architecture. Divide tenants or workloads across independent cells, each a full copy of the stack with no shared regional dependencies. A failure in one cell affects only the tenants assigned to it.

Staged deployments region by region. Roll changes out to one region at a time, with automated rollback when health checks fail, so a bad release stays in one region.

Static stability. Keep enough capacity running in each location to absorb a failure without launching instances or calling control plane APIs during the event, and use timeouts and circuit breakers so a degraded dependency does not cascade.

A second cloud provider for the most critical services. Running on two providers removes dependence on any one provider’s regional and global control planes. The operational cost is real, and it can be kept flat with one deployment workflow for both providers. See how to add a second cloud provider for failover without doubling your ops work and the cost of active-active vs active-passive.

Regulated industries face specific expectations here. See how financial services companies stay online during cloud outages.

Control Plane is the unbreakable platform for running production workloads. It runs serverless, standard, stateful, and cron workloads natively on AWS, GCP, and Azure, VM workloads on locations joined through Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes, and workloads on Kubernetes clusters you already run or your own machines, including on premises, active-active across regions and clouds.

A workload deployed to a GVC is active-active in every location of that GVC from one definition. Control Plane’s built-in global endpoint routes each request to the nearest healthy location, so failover is a routing change with no standby to start and no DNS change during the incident. Locations can be regions of one cloud, for example us-east-1 plus us-east-2 or us-west-2, or regions on AWS, GCP, and Azure together.

During the October 20, 2025 AWS us-east-1 outage, Control Plane customers with us-east-1 in their GVC had workloads active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds, according to Control Plane’s internal incident telemetry. About 20% of Control Plane customers had us-east-1 in their GVC.

Platform routing moves stateless traffic. Stateful recovery depends on your replication design. Control Plane’s template catalog includes a Postgres Multi-Location template that promotes a replica automatically when it spans three or more locations, and a CockroachDB template that survives the loss of one of three locations.

Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security. On Control Plane-managed locations there is no Kubernetes cluster to operate. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations. You pay for the CPU and memory a workload reserves, with no contracts or minimums. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant.

Short answers for teams planning for a us-east-1 or other regional outage.

They run critical services in more than one region or cloud before the outage, replicate data to the second location, and fail over with a rehearsed routing change or automated health checks that do not depend on us-east-1 control planes. Temporal, FireHydrant, LoginRadius, Block, and Ably published accounts of how their multi-region designs kept core services running during the October 2025 outage.

Map every dependency in your request path, run capacity in a second region or cloud, replicate data with measured lag, keep us-east-1-only control planes out of the failover path, and run game days that measure RTO and RPO. The 12-row checklist in this guide covers each step.

us-west-2 (Oregon) is geographically distant and offers broad service availability. us-east-2 (Ohio) is closer, so latency to us-east-1 is lower; Ably moved new connections from us-east-1 to us-east-2 during the October 2025 outage with a worst-case latency impact of 12 ms at p50. Any AWS region still depends on us-east-1 for IAM, Route 53, and CloudFront control plane operations (Route 53 accelerated recovery covers public record changes if you turn it on in advance), and many customers fail over to the same nearby regions at once, so reserve capacity in the region you choose.

The main cost drivers are capacity headroom, duplicated data stores, and cross-region data transfer for replication. Active-passive adds the cost of the warm capacity you keep in the recovery region. In a two-region active-active setup, each region must absorb full peak traffic if the other fails, unless the surviving region can scale up during the event; three or more locations reduce the headroom each one needs. Control Plane customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure.

For most teams, multi-region is the right first step, because it covers regional failures like the October 2025 us-east-1 event. A second cloud also covers failures of one provider’s global control planes. On Control Plane, one workload definition runs active-active in every location of its GVC, whether those are several regions of one cloud or regions on AWS, GCP, and Azure together.

Shift traffic away from the primary region in weighted steps during a low-traffic window, and at the same time block the recovery region’s outbound calls to primary-region endpoints with security groups, network ACLs, or AWS Fault Injection Service. The traffic shift tests routing, and the egress block exposes dependencies that still resolve to the primary region. Record time to full traffic shift, error rates, and replication lag at cutover. See how to test failover without taking production down.

Regional services shared by every zone. In October 2025 the trigger was the DNS record for the regional DynamoDB endpoint, and EC2 instance launches, Network Load Balancer health checks, Lambda, ECS, EKS, Fargate, and STS were impaired across the region. Global services with control planes in us-east-1, such as IAM, Route 53, and CloudFront, can also block changes during an event.

Control Plane’s Cloud Outage Tracker records 9 of AWS’s 14 major outages since 2020 in us-east-1, a count not adjusted for region size. Three us-east-1 events since October 2025 each lasted more than 13 hours: the October 19-20 regional event, the October 28 event affecting EC2 launches and ECS, and the May 2026 single-zone event.

Control plane operations create, change, or delete resources, such as creating an IAM role or updating a Route 53 record. Data plane operations use existing resources, such as answering a DNS query or authorizing a signed request. During a us-east-1 event, control plane operations for global services can be impaired while data plane operations usually continue, so a failover plan should rely on data plane operations.

A workload in a Control Plane GVC runs active-active in every location of that GVC, and the global endpoint routes each request to the nearest healthy location, so traffic shifts to the remaining locations automatically. See the October 2025 figures in How Control Plane fits.

To run your workloads active-active across regions and clouds, talk to the Control Plane team or sign up free.

#9872. I ran 3 Claude Code architecture diagram tools on my repo. Here's what each one got right

My project, worklore, is a small app that grew in all directions: a Python backend on AWS Lambda, a plain-JS site, an MCP connector for agents, and four more repos around it. I wanted a picture of it I could trust. So in one day I ran three open-source tools that turn code into a diagram or a map, all three as plugins for Claude Code:

Floorplan's README has a nice table comparing the three. It says what each tool answers and who it's for. It has no time, no cost and no pictures of the other two. This post fills that in, on one real codebase, and then does the test I actually care about: can each one answer real questions about my own code?

Floorplan read my 166 files and drew them as parts with plain-words descriptions. The first surprise: it found 0 endpoints. My server keeps its routes in one table keyed by "METHOD /path", not in a framework router. I opened a pull request to read that shape, and the author merged it 70 minutes later. Then it showed all 66.

The real trap was the user flows. While building the map, the agent also wrote flows, and it wrote them from its memory of my app. One said a person can publish a story from the website. The site can't do that. Another got wrong how a story gets drafted for someone else. A wrong flow and a right one look the same on the map.

What fixed it was a button Floorplan already has: Request a new flow. You describe a flow in plain words, and the agent traces it through the code, tying every step to a route or a function. I deleted the hand-written flows and requested 17. Then I ran 16 of them against a staging copy of my backend: 14 work, one partly, one can't be tested there. The 17th, a nightly job on my Mac, had been quietly failing for two nights.

I wrote it up step by step, so your agent can redo it on your app: My agent drew my app's user flows from memory and got two wrong; Floorplan's traced ones were right.

Archify draws from a JSON description and then checks it hard: every cited line must exist at the pinned commit, and the last check opens the diagram in a real browser. What its docs don't say up front: a diagram pins exactly one repository. My project lives in five, and the links between them aren't code at all. One repo is a skill that tells an agent to call my API with curl; another is a scanner my server keeps a copy of. A tool that follows imports sees five islands.

So I pinned the repo where the system runs, linked its boxes to lines of code, and drew the other repos as named boxes with a card saying what each holds. Two runs failed first: my SSH remote was rejected for web links (the HTTPS form works), and my uncommitted edits shifted line numbers away from the committed bytes Archify checks against.

Archify proves the cited lines exist. It does not prove what a card says. One of mine, "how stories get written", was wrong twice, again from my agent's memory. The full recipe: One architecture diagram for a project split across five repos, with Archify.

I ran Understand Anything headless, so I got exact numbers: 14 minutes, 16 helper agents working in batches of five, and $13.01 at API list prices (on a Claude subscription it comes out of your plan instead). Its README warns that the first run uses a lot of tokens. It does.

What you get is a lot: 732 nodes (files, functions, classes, config, docs), 1,625 links, 9 layers, and a 15-step tour that starts at the README and walks through the code in a sensible order. Every function has a one-line summary. I checked the summaries in the places where my agent had been wrong from memory, and they were right.

Two things to know before installing it. Its start-of-session hook tells the agent to rebuild a stale graph and "Do not ask the user for confirmation" (only if you turn auto-update on). And its dashboard runs as a local server; in a headless run it died after 10 minutes, when Claude Code stops background jobs.

It feels made for someone else's project: the tour and the summaries teach you a codebase you've never seen.

Pictures are nice. What I wanted was answers. I asked each tool the same three questions, the kind I'd ask before changing anything:

Floorplan got them in its Ask bar, Understand Anything in its chat command, and for Archify an agent that could see only the diagram. Then a plain agent with no map at all read the code to make an answer key.

Nobody made anything up, which already beats my agent's memory. But look at how they got there. Floorplan's Ask reads the map and the code, by design. Understand Anything's chat is meant to answer from the graph, yet it opened the source files anyway and said so. Archify has no way to answer questions, and the diagram simply doesn't hold this level of detail.

And the plain agent reading code found things none of the three did. The biggest was a security hole. When an AI app connects to worklore through OAuth, the sign-in advertised two permissions, worklore.read and worklore.write. The code never checked them. The app got an ordinary account pass, and that pass also worked on the site's REST API: it could delete my stories, change their visibility, and, since I'm the admin, open the admin pages. All three maps described the sign-in correctly, as a flow. None of them asked what the token could reach once issued, because that isn't a box or an arrow.

I fixed it before publishing this. An app's pass is now marked as one, works only through the connector, and only within what you approved; an app that asks only to read can't write. A new test walks the whole OAuth flow and then tries the pass on every kind of route.

The one habit that works with all three: before trusting a map, ask it three questions you already know the answers to. It takes two minutes and tells you which parts were traced and which were remembered.

Both write-ups above are on worklore as stories your agent can redo: what I tried, what failed, the exact steps, and how to check it worked. If you run either one on your own repo, the story page shows whether it worked for other people too.

#9870. Building Introworth: Pricing Attention Without Turning People Into Inventory — What Worked, What Broke

Posted on Nov 6 • Originally published at onelifevibe.blogspot.com

Most finance dashboards answer the wrong question. They show a single net worth number, big and green or red, and leave you to decide whether you are winning or failing that day.

Introworth was built around two quieter ideas. First, net worth is a trend line, not a verdict — a direction over months matters more than a snapshot on a bad Tuesday. Second, attention has value too. People give hours a day to platforms for free, and a tool that helps you think about your money should also help you notice what your time and attention are worth.

That is the product at Introworth — part of the OneLifeVibe family of sites.

The first version was deliberately small: a way to log assets and debts and see the trend, not just the total, plus a simple frame for valuing attention — what an hour of focused time returns, and where it leaks away for nothing. No trading, no advice engine, no leaderboard. The point was clarity, not gamification.

Keeping it small helped. A trend chart forces honest design choices: you have to handle months with missing data, debts that move slower than assets, and the fact that most real progress is boring and gradual. If the chart only looks good when numbers jump, the chart is lying.

Three things broke early, and all three were instructive.

First, people read the snapshot anyway. Even with a trend view front and centre, testers asked "so is that good?" about a single number. The fix was not more explanation — it was making the trend the headline and demoting the single figure to a supporting detail.

Second, valuing attention felt abstract until it was concrete. "Your attention is valuable" is a slogan. Showing someone that two hours a night of unfocused scrolling is, at even a modest hourly rate, a four-figure monthly leak — that lands. Concrete beats principled.

Third, signup friction cost more than any missing feature. Every extra field before someone sees their first trend line loses people who were curious but not committed. The fleet learned this across several sites: let people see the value first, ask for commitment second.

Honestly: small, and early. When the wider OneLifeVibe fleet was last counted in detail in late October, it had a few hundred users across all its sites, and Introworth was one of the smallest — single digits at that baseline count. No revenue claims, no growth chart that goes up and to the right.

That is exactly why the trend-line framing matters for building, too. A small product judged by a single day's snapshot always looks like a failure. Judged by direction — are the people who stay finding it clearer month over month, is the friction going down, is the core loop getting simpler — there is something real to work with.

Simpler onboarding, better handling of irregular months, and keeping the attention view grounded in a person's own numbers rather than generic rates. If that sounds unglamorous, it is. Most useful tools are.

If you are building a finance or attention tool, the transferable lesson is this: pick the frame before you pick the features. A verdict frame produces anxiety and churn. A trend frame produces patience — in users, and in the builder.

#9869. Bank statement PDFs to CSV, part 8: encrypted, stamped, and line-less — three edge cases I finally tested

Part 6 ended with a list of things this converter had not proven. One item on that list was three PDF shapes I had never tested: encrypted PDFs, image PDFs that still have a text layer, and statements with no table ruling lines at all. This post closes that item. Two of the three went fine. The third found a real limitation, and that is the most useful part.

The test setup is the same as the rest of the series: synthetic fixtures, invented payees and amounts, ground truth written down before the converter runs. The new fixtures are E1, E2 and E3 in the repository, all built from the same 12-row statement as fixture A, so the results compare directly.

I took fixture A and re-saved it with AES-256 encryption (user password test123 — a synthetic fixture, nothing secret in it). Before this round, the converter's answer was bad: pdfplumber raised a PdfminerException with an empty message, wrapping pdfminer's PDFPasswordIncorrect, and the CLI printed a bare traceback. A user would have learned nothing from that output.

The fix is small and now tested: extract_transactions translates that specific failure into a PasswordProtectedError with a plain message — the PDF is password-protected, decrypt it first, then convert — and the CLI exits with code 2, no traceback, and writes no CSV. The GUI already turned every failure into a human message; its technical-reason line is no longer empty for this case either. The converter still cannot open an encrypted PDF. What changed is that it now says so clearly instead of crashing obscurely.

Real statements often carry a raster stamp or logo on the same page as the transaction table. I embedded a small raster stamp image ("business seal") in the top-right corner of page 1, leaving the text layer untouched, and ran the same 12 rows through.

Result: 12/12 rows, every field correct, identical to fixture A. An embedded image does not disturb table extraction, because pdfplumber reads the text layer and the image is simply not text. This was the expected outcome; it is worth having as a test rather than an assumption, since the converter will meet stamped statements in the real world.

This is the interesting one. I drew the same 12 rows at the same column positions, with the same header, but no table lines whatsoever. Without lines, pdfplumber finds no table, and the converter falls back to its line parser, which reads each row as a line of text: date, description, then the numbers.

Result: 12/12 rows found, 12/12 dates correct — but only 2 of the 12 rows are fully correct. The 10 spending rows came back with debit and credit swapped.

The reason is structural, not a typo. In this fixture the debit and credit are separate columns with unsigned amounts — 328.50 in the debit column, no minus sign. The line parser sees two trailing numbers (amount, balance) and, with no sign to go on, assigns the amount to income. The table path never has this problem, because the header tells it which column is which; the line fallback has no column information at all.

I locked this in as a characterisation test — it asserts the measured behaviour, 2 fully correct out of 12, with the 10 swaps — so the limitation is on the record and any future fix has to update the test deliberately. The fix would be to give the fallback column positions, for example by reading word x-coordinates instead of plain text lines. That is real work and out of scope for presale v1, so for now the honest statement is: statements without ruling lines extract, but spending and income may be swapped. The two income rows were correct, which is consistent with the mechanism, not luck.

The three shapes were tested on synthetic fixtures, not real bank PDFs — real statements with the same shapes are still untested, as are real bank samples in general. The Windows installer still has no real-machine install check, and there is still no auto-update. Those items stay on the list from part 6.

Links: the converter repository is at https://github.com/alapha888/bank-statement-presale, and the presale page is at https://alapha888.github.io/bank-statement-presale/.

#9868. The Zero-Budget AI Launch Playbook: 80% of Your Launch Happens Before Launch Day

Host of GTM Works. Writing about AI products, go-to-market, and growth.

Host of GTM Works. Writing about AI products, go-to-market, and growth.

Host of GTM Works. Writing about AI products, go-to-market, and growth.

Part 1 of 2: How to earn attention from Reddit, Hacker News and Product Hunt when you have no ad budget

Try this thought experiment. You have a good idea for an AI product. How long before someone else ships something nearly identical?

A year ago the honest answer was a few months. Today, with Claude Code, Cursor and a dozen other tools, it's closer to a long weekend. You can polish the model, sand down the UX, tune the prompts. Competitors can do all of that too, and they'll do it faster than you'd like.

What they can't copy overnight is who already knows you exist: the communities that trust you, the search results that surface you, the people who will say your name when someone asks "what should I use for this?" That's distribution, and it's still stubbornly human work.

I come from a growth background and have worked on go-to-market for several AI products: a music generator, an AI companion app, a financial-data platform, and a few others. I've done launches with money and without it. Some of them worked. Some of them got my accounts banned. This two-part series is the playbook I wish I'd had at the start, with the failures left in.

Part 1 is about the launch itself and the three communities most founders obsess over: Reddit, Hacker News and Product Hunt. Part 2 covers search, PR, creators and the art of making noise.

When I picture "launching a product," my brain reaches for the standard toolkit: buy promotion, record a slick demo video, line up a wave of creators to post the same demo on the same day with the same script, and manufacture the feeling that this thing is blowing up.

That's a valid playbook, and I'll get to it. But it hides the most important fact about launches: the visible event is the tip of the iceberg.

Take Product Hunt. Whether your product climbs the daily ranking has very little to do with what you do that day. It depends on whether, months earlier, you quietly gathered people who care. We live in an attention economy where everyone is distracted by something else, so the traffic and noise you capture on launch day are a function of the groundwork underneath.

The same goes for offline. A great launch is rarely purely online. It leans on the founder friends you met at a conference, the developers you traded favors with, the investor who happily retweets your news. These threads connect to each other, and none of them can be pulled out of thin air the week before.

So the first reframe: stop asking "how do I launch?" and start asking "what can I build in the 90 days before the launch that makes launch day easy?"

If I could only give you one principle, it would be this: share the value, not your product.

In marketing terms: give first, collect later. Put something genuinely useful in front of people before you ask for anything. Don't expect anyone to use your product in return. They have alternatives, they owe you nothing, and they can smell an agenda from the first sentence.

I'll keep returning to this idea, because it shows up everywhere: in how you post on Reddit, how you write comments, how you build an audience, how you approach creators, even how you make friends at conferences. The tactics change by channel. The rule doesn't.

It also changes how fast you should move. Value-first marketing is slow by design. If you're in a hurry, you'll be tempted to skip straight to the ask, and the channels below are very good at punishing that.

Product Hunt is where most founders start, so let's be honest about what it has become.

The best example I know of a good Product Hunt launch is Gamma, the AI presentation tool. As I remember it, they spent a long time building up a large group of loyal early users before they launched, back when Product Hunt's credibility was still intact. On launch day they rallied those users, and the upvotes were real: actual customers vouching for a product they already liked. That's the model. The ranking was the result of earlier work, not a substitute for it.

Today the picture is murkier, for three reasons:

My suggestion: treat Product Hunt as an optional credibility badge, not your launch. If you already have a base of users who will show up and vouch for you organically, go for it, and choose a calm day. If you don't, spend those weeks building the base.

My team and I have launched on both Product Hunt and Hacker News, and I find Hacker News the more community-driven of the two. It's run by Y Combinator, and it is famously hard to game. If you're thinking about creating a stack of accounts to push a post up the front page, don't bother.

Three things I'd tell anyone planning a Hacker News post:

1. Start building your account months ahead. If you want to share an article or a launch there someday, begin now. Spend three or four months commenting thoughtfully on other people's posts and becoming a recognizable voice. You can't suddenly decide on launch week to do something promotional. The community leans technical and pure, and it reacts badly to anything that smells like marketing.

2. Reputation is what keeps a post alive. If you've made real friends in the community and respected regulars comment on your post, it stays visible far longer. Without that, it sinks quickly.

3. Interesting beats technical. You don't need to publish hardcore engineering to get noticed. When we were working on an AI music product, ChatGPT went down one day. We wrote a song about the outage and shared it. It caught fire on Hacker News, a small but very real win. The bonus came afterwards: a number of people who write technical blogs saw it and linked to our song from their own posts, which handed us several natural backlinks for free.

That last part is worth sitting with. We didn't set out to win backlinks. We made something people wanted to share, and the SEO benefit came as a by-product. That's value-first marketing in miniature.

If you have a small budget or none at all, Reddit is the channel I'd look at first, but only if you can start two to three months early to build up karma and a credible profile.

One warning before the tactics: don't outsource your posts to someone else's accounts. Only the founder really knows what the product feels like, and many "we'll post for you" accounts just generate generic AI-written content that readers sniff out immediately.

Write a genuine comparison of your product and similar tools. Be fair. Cover the pros and cons of your competitors as well as your own, and write as a user of AI tools rather than as the company.

Then post it in small, niche subreddits with a few hundred to a few thousand members, ideally ones whose rules aren't strict about self-promotion. Avoid the giant communities. Their moderators have seen every flavor of disguised promotion and will remove it.

Why bother if the audience is tiny? Because the goal isn't Reddit traffic. It's two long-tail effects:

The mistake people make is wanting both: a comparison post and thousands of eyeballs, so they post it in a huge subreddit and get it removed. Pick one goal.

Posts are slow and risky. Comments are underrated.

This only works if your profile looks like a real community member's and not a billboard. Participate in discussions that have nothing to do with your product.

If you do want to post, make it beneficial to others first. In my experience, the posts that have done well for me, reaching tens of thousands of views and thousands of upvotes, all shared something useful and weren't ads.

Building an AI music product? Share your favorite playlists, artists or recent releases in the right music community. Building an AI travel product? Share routes. Weaving your product into a post in a natural way is tricky, so don't force it.

And here's the pattern that works: be consistent. Post the same kind of thing on a schedule, say one or two playlists a week. For the first four weeks, mention nothing about your product. Let people get used to you as the person who brings good music. Only when the community knows you can you say, "By the way, I'm building this, and it tries to solve that." By then it feels like a friend sharing news.

Reddit communities care deeply about their atmosphere. If people recognize you as someone who adds value, they upvote you and thank you in the comments. If not, you're gone.

The lesson is the one I started with: you can't extract value from a community before you've put some in.

The cheapest launch I've ever run started months before there was a product to launch.

We were building a data platform, something like a Bloomberg-style terminal where people can explore all kinds of data. The question every founder in that position asks is: where do the first users come from?

My answer was to build a media publication in parallel with the product. While the platform was being developed, the publication used its data to write analysis: price trends, macroeconomic outlooks, that kind of thing. Readers found the articles useful enough to forward to friends, and they spread well in several markets. At the bottom of each piece, we invited readers into a private community (a Discord server, for readers outside China).

The whole thing cost almost nothing. It worked because the content and the product were tightly connected: the articles were made from the product's data, so every reader was already a qualified prospect.

If you take one idea from this section, take this: find the valuable thing your product makes possible and give that away publicly, long before you ask for a signup.

Everyone wants the shortcut: the viral post, the front-page ranking, the one tweet that changes everything. Sometimes shortcuts exist. But the launches that hold up are the ones that look like overnight successes and turn out to be slow, boring groundwork on the inside.

Give first. Be patient. Show up in the places where your users already are, as one of them.

In Part 2, I'll cover the other half of the playbook: starting SEO on day one with long-tail keywords, using PR to build authority (including with AI search), working with creators without wasting money, and what to make of the rising wave of attention-grabbing stunts, including the cautionary side of the story.

#9865. The best apples for apple pie: Here's how to choose.: We put six varieties to the test.

Which are the best pie apples? With apple-picking season hard upon us, it's time to dust off your favorite apple pie recipe, sharpen your crust-rolling skills, and get ready to enjoy fall's favorite dessert: apple pie.

You may be tempted to make your pie from one of the six apple varieties that dominate the domestic market year-round: Red Delicious, Golden Delicious, Gala, Fuji, Granny Smith, and McIntosh.

But when fall rolls around, farmers' markets and orchard farm stands offer an abundance of apple choices.

You've probably identified your favorite eating apple. But what about the best pie apples? They're not necessarily the same. Red and Golden Delicious, for instance, are reliably crisp, sweet-eating apples. But when you bake them into a pie, they can become mushy and lose some of their sweetness. So what are the best apples for pie?

We'll put six different pie apples to the test.

The pie apples: I decide to put two of my favorites, Golden Russet and Northern Spy, up against a couple of classic pie apples: McIntosh and Cortland. I also add Granny Smith because, if there's one ubiquitous, year-round apple, Granny Smith is it. Ginger Gold — a Golden Delicious cross with Albemarle Pippin — is another variety that's often available in fall, and a worthy representative of the Delicious family.

And yes, there are plenty of other apple varieties to choose from: Fuji, Gala, Honey Crisp, and so many more. But with limited time and resources — and a pan with space for just six pies — I'm not able to test every apple out there. But if you want to choose the best pie apples among your personal favorites, you can have fun doing this same test at home.

I use a muffin tin to bake apples sweetened with a bit of sugar. To mimic apple pie (sans crust), I pile sliced apples high in the pan. Then I bake them in a preheated 425°F oven for 20 minutes, lower the oven temperature to 375°F, and continue to bake the apples until they're bubbly, about 40 minutes.

I had no idea there'd be such significant differences in both texture and flavor. For example, Russets and Macs are sweetened with the same amount of sugar, bake at the same temperature, for the same amount of time —  and offer way different results.

So, Granny Smith looks like the best combination of both taste and texture. Does it make the very best apple pie?

Not necessarily. I've baked many pies with this all-purpose apple, especially during the winter when other apples are scarce or pricey. A pie made 100% with Granny Smith apples is a mighty fine pie. But in fall, when every apple variety in the world is seemingly at your fingertips, why not take advantage of one or two (or more) of your own local favorites?

At the end of the day, choosing the best pie apples is a personal decision. My best apple pie would include a combination of these three: Cortland, for flavor; Russet, for texture; and Granny Smith, for its combination of the two.

What apples would fill your best pie? Bake your favorite varieties side by side and see what happens; the results may surprise you.

Please share your favorite apples for pie — and your favorite apple pie tips! — in comments, below.

#9863. The $50 Million Gamble That Made Red Bull Marketing History

Hi, I'm Yukti Sachan, a writer and content creator from India with an interest in storytelling, books, marketing, and formula 1

Hi, I'm Yukti Sachan, a writer and content creator from India with an interest in storytelling, books, marketing, and formula 1

Hi, I'm Yukti Sachan, a writer and content creator from India with an interest in storytelling, books, marketing, and formula 1

Imagine someone asks you, “Hey, do you want to jump from the edge of space?”

Your first response would probably be, “What the hell is wrong with you?”

But when that exact question was asked to Felix Baumgartner, he basically went, “Yeah, sure. Why not?”

Now, you might be wondering who on Earth was crazy enough to ask that question in the first place.

Ladies and gentlemen, this is the story of the Red Bull Stratos mission: a man crazy enough to jump from the edge of space, a company crazy enough to fund it, and a PR gamble that somehow paid off spectacularly.

Quick disclaimer: Everything you’re about to read comes from me spending the last few hours buried in articles, reports, and marketing resources because apparently that’s what I do for fun now. I tried reading an actual marketing textbook, but it made me question reality, so I fled to Wikipedia, reports, and other resources instead. If I get something wrong, please let me know! Constructive corrections are always welcome—I like learning more than pretending I’m right.

Enough corporate jargon. Let's throw a man out of space.

Now switch the M and the E, and you get Max Emilian Verstappen—okay, that’s not how names work. You get Max Verstappen. But let’s not get distracted.

Earned Media Value (EMV) is the estimated dollar value of publicity a brand receives without paying for it directly.

“The estimated dollar equivalent of unpaid public exposure.”

Which is technically correct, but sounds like a corporate robot wrote it.

So here’s the version my brain understands:

You do something. People can’t stop talking about it. You didn’t pay them to talk about it. That’s EMV.

Influencers posting because they genuinely found something cool? EMV.

People sending the campaign to their friends? EMV.

Yeah... people are definitely going to talk about that.

A simplified formula looks something like this:

EMV = (Total Impressions × Industry CPM) ÷ 1,000

Basically, it estimates how much money the brand would have had to spend on advertising to achieve the same amount of attention.

Some companies also factor in engagement, audience quality, creator influence, and even audience sentiment. After all, ten million people saying, “This campaign is brilliant,” and ten million people saying, “This campaign is terrible,” are two very different outcomes.

Because it lets them estimate the value of all the buzz they generated without paying directly for every conversation.

Imagine your campaign gets millions of people talking. If buying that same amount of attention through traditional advertising would’ve cost millions of dollars, that’s exactly what EMV is trying to estimate.

It isn’t money sitting in Red Bull’s bank account.

It’s simply a way of estimating the advertising value of the attention they earned.

Compared to EMV, ROI is wonderfully straightforward.

ROI simply measures how much profit (or loss) you made compared to how much you invested.

ROI = (Net Profit ÷ Cost of Investment) × 100

Suppose you invest $1,000 into something.

That means your investment generated a 50% return.

A positive ROI means your investment made money.

(Or, as I like to call it, congratulations—you’ve invented a very expensive hobby.)

So what’s the difference between EMV and ROI?

EMV asks: “How valuable was all the attention we earned?”

ROI asks: “Did we actually make money compared to what we spent?”

The other measures financial performance.

We’ll need both of these in a minute because Red Bull Stratos wasn’t just an engineering miracle.

And that's exactly why Red Bull Stratos is still taught as one of the greatest marketing campaigns ever executed.

Somewhere inside Red Bull, on what was probably a completely normal Tuesday, someone had a thought.

A completely normal thought, according to Red Bull standards. Which is already slightly concerning, because Red Bull’s definition of “normal” has historically been questionable.

“Everyone is doing television commercials, right?”

Then came the question that changed everything:

At the time, YouTube livestreaming was still a relatively new idea. Instead of buying a traditional advertising slot, Red Bull could create something people would actively choose to watch.

What could possibly be big enough to capture the world’s attention?

“What if a man jumped from the stratosphere?”

Now, most companies would probably stop here and call it a concerning brainstorming session.

Red Bull looked at the idea and apparently said:

And just like that, Red Bull Stratos was born.

With an estimated investment of around $50 million, Red Bull wasn’t simply funding a stunt. They were funding a scientific mission, an engineering challenge, and one of the boldest marketing gambles in history.

Fifty million dollars is the kind of money that makes normal people rethink buying a coffee.

Red Bull looked at that amount and thought:

“Perfect. Let’s use it to make a human being fall from the sky.”

Unlike certain Formula 1 teams that shall remain unnamed (Ferrari, I’m looking at you), Red Bull actually had a plan.

An Austrian skydiver with years of experience performing extreme jumps, Felix was not exactly someone who looked at a dangerous idea and immediately walked away.

When Red Bull approached him with the idea of jumping from the stratosphere, his reaction was essentially:

Which is either the bravest sentence ever spoken or the sentence responsible for several safety engineers losing sleep.

But this wasn’t just a man standing on a platform and falling.

Behind that jump were scientists, engineers, safety experts, pressure suits, a specially designed capsule, and a massive helium balloon carrying Felix nearly 39 kilometers above Earth.

Basically, hundreds of extremely intelligent people worked together to make sure one person could safely do something that sounded like a rejected cartoon plot.

On October 14, 2012, Felix Baumgartner stepped out of his capsule approximately 39 kilometers above Earth.

During his free fall, he reached a maximum speed of around 1,357 km/h, making him the first person to break the sound barrier during a free fall.

The entire event was livestreamed, from the balloon launch to the moment Felix stepped into the unknown.

This was not a commercial people had to sit through before watching something else.

This was the thing people wanted to watch.

The jump itself lasted around 10 minutes, with approximately 4 minutes and 20 seconds spent in free fall before his parachute opened.

What looked like a man simply falling from the sky was actually years of preparation, engineering, testing, and scientific collaboration.

Red Bull had spent years preparing for a moment that would last only a few minutes.

But those few minutes had the potential to become one of the greatest marketing successes ever created.

Because this was not a pre-recorded commercial where a company could quietly delete the footage and pretend nothing happened.

And the internet, famously known for being calm and reasonable during unexpected events, was waiting.

If something went wrong, millions of people would see it happen in real time.

Red Bull wasn’t just risking $50 million.

They had spent years preparing for a moment that would last only a few minutes.

And then Felix stepped out of the capsule.

At no point during the livestream did Felix stop mid-free fall, pull out a can of Red Bull, take a sip, and say,

“Look at me! I’m literally flying through the stratosphere!”

Because he was wearing a Red Bull-branded pressure suit.

The massive helium balloon carrying him nearly 39 kilometres into the sky?

They didn’t interrupt people’s attention.

Nobody tuned in because they wanted to watch an advertisement.

“Oh my God. Someone is actually going to jump from the edge of space.”

Humans have a fascinating habit of stopping to watch extraordinary things unfold.

When something unbelievable happens, people naturally gather around it.

Instead of asking millions of people to spend thirty seconds watching their advertisement...

...they created something millions of people willingly spent hours watching.

And the brand just happened to own that moment.

Because Red Bull has never really sold caffeine.

They’ve sold the idea that normal is boring.

People don’t buy Red Bull because it’s simply an energy drink.

They buy into everything the brand represents.

Whether that’s Formula 1, cliff diving, mountain biking, air races, or a man casually deciding gravity is optional.

Then the internet did what the internet does best.

Friends sending each other the livestream.

Every conversation became free advertising.

Exactly what we talked about earlier with Earned Media Value.

Nearly eight million people watched simultaneously on YouTube.

Hundreds of millions watched clips afterwards.

The campaign generated an estimated $6 billion in earned media value.

Red Bull didn’t interrupt millions of people to tell them they were exciting.

They did something so exciting that millions of people interrupted their own lives to watch.

How Red Bull Accidentally Built One of the Most Successful Media Empires in Sport
