#9862. ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation

💻 Code | 📊 Data | 🤖 Models | 📖 Documentation

Robots are learning to fold laundry, sort parts, and handle unfamiliar objects. But those demonstrations are often rather narrow and don't explain what a robot has learned or why it fails.

To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure.

Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control.

Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks: an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking.

ToyBlocks automatically generates demonstrations, which are recordings of a robot completing tasks in simulation, without requiring time-consuming teleoperation, in which a person remotely controls the robot. Researchers can easily vary these training experiences. For example, a team could generate more pushing or flipping demonstrations, then evaluate performance on tasks kept out of training.

Starting with ToyBlocks as our first FoundationWorld, we aim to extend the approach to increasingly complex environments.

Building on our earlier work in open robot learning, including MolmoAct 2, MolmoBot, and MolmoSpaces, ToyBlocks gives researchers a way to study robotics questions in a deliberately constrained domain.

As a FoundationWorld, ToyBlocks is designed around four requirements: (1) realistic physics and appearance, (2) automatic generation of tasks and demonstrations at scale, (3) challenges that combine reasoning with dexterity, and (4) broad coverage of the tasks possible within a domain.

Open-ended domains require modeling a wide range of objects and interactions, making it infeasible to fulfill all these requirements. ToyBlocks’ narrow scope, on the other hand, makes it possible to fulfill them all.

Within ToyBlocks' smaller setting, researchers can work toward investigating how a robot can learn to perform any reasonable task while being confident that the simulated arm and blocks behave very similarly to their physical counterparts.

A physical robot gripper above wooden blocks in the ToyBlocks setup.

ToyBlocks is not just about picking and stacking blocks: pictures and letters on the blocks' faces allow for searching, sorting, and arranging tasks. A robot may need to turn a block to see a hidden face before deciding where it belongs. Domain randomization – varying block size, table height, and other physical properties from scene to scene – tests how well models generalize as the geometry changes.

ToyBlocks automatically generates skills (behaviors for short tasks) and task demonstrations that can be used to train models or adapt previously trained models through additional training (fine-tuning). High-level reasoning models decide what to do; low-level action models control the robot’s movements. The framework can also be used to easily design experiments and validate hypotheses.

ToyBlocks uses reinforcement learning (RL) and motion planning, which computes how the robot should move, to generate skills for short-horizon tasks, which involve brief sequences of actions. Skill training takes place in Isaac Lab, Nvidia's open-source framework for robot learning in simulation. Through trial and error, these policies – models that choose the robot’s actions – learn non-prehensile skills such as pushing a block across the table or flipping it onto another face without picking it up. Skill generation can draw on privileged information – values the simulator can supply directly but a real robot cannot, such as a block's exact position and orientation – instead of estimating it from camera images. This enables the automatic generation of skills that would require teleoperation in the real world.

To generate demonstration data, a task-and-motion planner (TAMP) automatically selects and sequences the skills needed to solve a task and plans the robot’s movements between them. Running each plan in simulation produces a dataset of recorded demonstrations along with labels describing which task or skill the robot performs. ToyBlocks scales data generation through generating and executing hundreds of such plans in parallel on a single graphics processing unit (GPU), reaching up to 24 times real-time performance.

Acting from sensor observations adds a perception problem: a model has to estimate a block’s pose – its position and orientation – which the simulator could supply directly. To reflect real-world conditions, ToyBlocks trains models that map raw sensor observations to actions.

Execution of Molmo 2 (a high-level model) and ManiFlow (a low-level model) trained in ToyBlocks. Molmo 2 selects skills such as rotation and flipping, indicating the relevant block via a pointing interface, while ManiFlow controls the simulated arm to execute the commanded skills.

ToyBlocks' controllable data generator lets users create training mixtures that emphasize particular skills or fill gaps in existing datasets. Researchers can study how much data a model needs and which experiences help it generalize to unseen tasks. For example, they could test whether adding rotation and pick-and-place demonstrations improves flipping, or vary the balance of examples inside and outside a defined workspace region—evaluating their choices on tasks kept out of training. Importantly, evaluation of trained models generates metrics beyond success rates; it provides information such as execution speeds, forces exerted on objects, and task progress measured via the same specifications used by the planning module.

A webpage interface lets users connect Claude – or another frontier model – and use natural language to instruct the robot or try tasks, offering a way to explore how a model plans and acts without needing robotics expertise.

The evaluations below use ToyBlocks to study how training data and methods affect performance, spatial reasoning, generalization to new letters and block appearances, multi-step planning, transfer to physical robots, and frontier models that act through tools. Users can easily design their own tasks and measures to investigate other questions—for example, whether a model performs better when it selects objects by pointing or by issuing text commands such as "pick the yellow block."

Low-level action models, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs), map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions.

The premise of VLAs is that, by pretraining on large-scale datasets, they can rapidly generalize to different scenarios or a specific workspace. However, evidence on how well these action models generalize remains conflicting. Some studies report that these action models are brittle to changes in inputs, such as different object layouts and lighting, whereas others show that VLAs generalize well. We argue that these studies often rely on real-world datasets with limited flexibility in spatial variations. ToyBlocks enables us to test how well action models generalize in a simple, easily reproducible setting with meaningful task-space diversity.

We design generalization tests that vary the skill sequences needed to complete an instruction, the letters or colors on the blocks, and the number of blocks in a scene. A stacking study can withhold four-block stacks from training, then test whether a model can combine familiar movements to build them. Workspace studies distinguish performance at new positions within a training region from performance beyond its boundaries, where the model has to extrapolate. We illustrate the study setup and findings below.

We consider four tasks: Stack, Unstack, Flip, and Rotate. For these tasks, we study interpolation (new configurations within the training range) and extrapolation (configurations beyond that range). For example, we evaluate generalization by training on scenarios where objects spawn only in the left region (green) and testing on the right region (orange), or by training on stack heights of 2 and 5 blocks and testing on heights 3 and 4.

Spatial generalization studies for VLA models (results based on ManiFlow, π0.5, and MolmoAct 2). Despite large-scale pretraining, these popular action models generalize poorly in the initial results. We improve generalization and analyze the contribution of each technique. The chart’s LoRA label stands for low-rank adaptation, a method for fine-tuning a model with a small set of trainable weight updates. We believe action model generalization remains far from solved; ToyBlocks provides a valuable testbed for systematically exploring generalization techniques.

Long-horizon tasks, which require many steps, allow us to measure how well models can plan a sequence of actions to solve them. Our framework enables us to create such long-horizon tasks, and create oracles – reference components that provide correct plans or actions – at both the high and low levels. This allows us to isolate whether the high-level planning or low-level execution failed when a model fails at a task. An example long-horizon task might be to spell “Ai2” with a block stack; because the letters may not be immediately visible, the agent must first choose actions that reveal information, and then plan and execute a sequence of actions to build the stack.

We evaluate hierarchical models with explicit high-level planning and low-level execution models. In this instance, we choose Molmo 2, a vision-language model (VLM), as the high-level planner, and ManiFlow as the low-level policy. Molmo 2 chooses the skill to execute and the block to execute it on, while the low-level model executes the instruction. We train low-level models such as ManiFlow to pause after completing the execution and query the high-level model for the next instruction. We evaluate the model’s planning abilities on three scenarios of increasing difficulty. The easiest scenario initializes with each character upright and facing the camera. The medium scenario has characters that may not be upright, and the hardest scenario contains characters that are not visible at the start of the episode.

Success rates on three-letter block-spelling tasks using Molmo 2 as the high-level reasoning model and either ManiFlow or a motion planner for low-level manipulation. An example task is “Stack Ai2”. Molmo 2 and ManiFlow are trained on ToyBlocks and evaluated across three difficulty settings and two generalization conditions.

Our experiments with agentic systems test how frontier models plan and act through tool calls. We study three settings using Claude Opus 5.5. In the search-and-spell setting, we expose ToyBlocks skills through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard for connecting AI applications to tools. The agent sees the scene through camera images, calls skills such as pick, flip, or rotate by pointing at a pixel, and decides when to search, build, or declare the task complete or impossible. The same MCP tools can execute either the scripted skills that generate ToyBlocks demonstrations (motion-planned pick and place, plus RL-based rotate and flip) or learned ManiFlow skills. ToyBlocks includes the framework behind these experiments, which also powers the natural-language web interface described earlier.

A frontier model (Claude Fable 5.1) controls a robot in a ToyBlocks world to search for and stack blocks into a tower spelling “Ai2.” During the episode, the agent muses, “I need to figure out whether pick-and-place naturally straightens orientation or if I need to correct it manually… I have 63 calls left, plenty to run a controlled test” (0:06). The agent later hypothesizes: “…maybe the gripper’s yaw is radial—pointing from the robot base toward the block” (0:15) and eventually confirms this hypothesis (0:26) before constructing the three-block tower, but the ‘A’ is sideways (1:11). Surprisingly, current frontier models often make similar perceptual errors (see the next figure), despite their impressive planning, spatial reasoning, and search capabilities.

For classical planning, the agent (our system using Claude Opus 5.5 to plan and choose actions) solves all 30 of a group of block-stacking tasks similar to ones that frontier models struggled with a few years ago, using text descriptions. It also solves 30 out of 30 while repeatedly observing camera images and choosing its next action in a closed loop.

In the search-and-spell setting, the agent had to generate stacks spelling out three-letter words. It had to find the blocks with the corresponding letters among up to eight blocks in the scene. Importantly, 50% of the scenes did not have blocks with all the required letters, rendering the task infeasible. In this case, we required the agent to state that the task is infeasible. We found that in this experiment, the agent was able to successfully solve or correctly declare infeasible 63% of the tasks. Errors were mostly caused by the agent confusing letters with look-alike letters (13%) or choosing an incorrect orientation for a letter in a stack (15%).

Our results also show that the agent was able to solve the task more efficiently when the blocks had semantic regularities, or patterns, taking advantage of such patterns to reason about occluded faces. For instance, in most of the infeasible scenes, when the blocks had no patterns, the agent correctly looked at all the blocks’ faces before declaring infeasibility, whereas it was able to declare infeasibility significantly faster when the blocks had semantic patterns.

Our third experimental setting asks whether an agent can learn how its skills behave, using experiments as a scientist would. When a skill behaves unexpectedly, the agent forms a hypothesis, designs a small test, and revises its understanding from the result. We expand on this idea by having an agent run its own experiments and write its own skill descriptions based on what it finds. These learned descriptions raise success rates from 24% with the default descriptions to 63%, outperforming the 36% achieved with descriptions written by a human expert.

Share of letter-block faces the agent had exposed by the end of each “search and spell” episode (bars averaged over 20 episodes; one marker per episode, styled by outcome). In a feasible task every letter of the three-letter target word is present; in an infeasible task, one letter is missing and the agent should say so. Each patterned block carries uppercase and lowercase instances of a letter, plus images that begin with the letter (e.g., A-block: apple, ant, A, 1, airplane, a); an unpatterned block’s six faces are randomized and unrelated. Correct: the tower spelled the word, or for infeasible tasks, the agent correctly declared the task impossible. Letter rotated or look-alike: the agent built the tower, but a letter was turned or a look-alike substituted, including five infeasible tasks declared solved with a look-alike in the missing letter’s place. Block fell out of reach; reported: a needed block was pushed out of the arm’s reach, so the agent reported that its task had become impossible. No report: the agent used up its motor-skill budget and stopped without claiming either outcome. With patterned blocks, the agent finishes having seen fewer faces, because it can infer what hidden faces must depict rather than checking every one.

Action-conditioned world models are trained to predict how a scene changes in response to a robot’s actions. Using them as an alternative to model-based simulators for training and evaluating robot policies is an active area of research. How well they serve this purpose depends on how accurately they predict physical interactions, which is hard to measure without knowing the true state of the scene. ToyBlocks provides this ground truth – the actual simulated scene state – enabling highly controlled tests of how recently developed world models perform in low-level object manipulation. Here, the arm’s end effector is its gripper.

Specifically, we tested whether action-conditioned world models are capable of predicting the motions of blocks or the outcomes of skill executions after being trained on example executions. To do so, we chose four different skills (pick-and-place, flip, rotate, and a mixed task) and generated 900 trajectories – sequences of robot states and actions over time – for each skill. 50% of these trajectories were successful demonstrations of the skill, and 50% were unsuccessful because of small changes to spatial configurations. With equal numbers of successful and unsuccessful executions, a model that always predicts success would be correct only half the time. The models were fine-tuned on these demonstrations and then tested on their ability to predict the outcome of action sequences of the same skills.

We find that Wan 2.2 predicts block motion and task outcomes most accurately. Astra tracks the gripper well but struggles to simulate contact. LeWM is fast and more accurate over short interaction segments, though it drifts over full trajectories. In additional experiments, we also showed that models that score higher on pose and success prediction also produce better training data: adding 100 model-generated trajectories (rollouts) from the best video-generation model raises a policy’s success in an unseen region from 19% to 78%.

We tested three types of models: a video prediction model with 5 billion parameters (Wan 2.2), an agentic model that created its own physics simulator tuned to match the demonstration data (Astra), and a latent world model (LeWM). During testing, each trained model has to predict future images, simulator states, or latent states (learned internal representations), respectively, based on an initial image and a sequence of actions. For full trajectories, models use the initial image as the only observed image, along with the action sequence. For short interaction segments – a single pick, place, flip, or rotate – models start from the real image immediately before that interaction. Full trajectories show how errors accumulate over long horizons, while interaction segments isolate a single interaction, such as the gripper making contact with a block, and show how well the model predicts it. To compare models fairly, we probe each model’s predictions, reading out where it expects the blocks and gripper to be at different points in the trajectory and whether it expects the task to succeed at the end.

Sim-to-real evaluations test policies trained in simulation on physical robots performing block manipulation tasks. By comparing simulation and real-world execution, we assess whether behaviors and failure patterns observed in simulation provide meaningful indications of real-world performance. For example, researchers can evaluate individual skills and their composition in longer-horizon tasks to identify where failures arise and whether these patterns carry over to physical deployments.

We test whether the models trained entirely on ToyBlocks simulation datasets can be deployed in the real world zero-shot, without training on real-world examples. We evaluate ManiFlow and each low-level skill (pick, place, flip, and rotate) individually. We test whether the hierarchical system (Molmo 2 + ManiFlow) can complete long-horizon three-block spelling tasks requiring sequences of these actions. Real-world experiments use a Franka FR3 arm with a Robotiq gripper across thirty scene configurations. Each scene contains 4–10 blocks seen during training. An episode is successful only if the relevant blocks are moved to target poses without collisions. If the operator intervenes to stop the robot due to an unsafe motion during an episode, it is marked as a failure.

ManiFlow’s atomic-skill success rates were similar in simulation and the real world (80.0% and 81.1%). The hierarchical Molmo 2 + ManiFlow system succeeded in 55.5% of simulated episodes (111/200) and 50.0% of real-world episodes (15/30); further trials are needed to establish statistical confidence across tasks.

Success rates of the ManiFlow low-level model and the hierarchical Molmo 2–ManiFlow system in simulation and the real world. For ManiFlow, the total count represents individual skill executions (pick, place, flip, and rotate), whereas for Molmo 2–ManiFlow, it represents block-spelling task episodes. The Molmo 2–ManiFlow evaluations use the easiest scene configuration defined in the simulation evaluation, with block characters visible and upright.

Side-by-side real-world and simulated block-stacking executions using the same high-level planner. Pink rings mark the planner’s target point for each skill. The scenes use different block labels, and simulation playback is retimed to align grasps and releases with the real robot.

To transfer Molmo 2 and ManiFlow – both trained exclusively on ToyBlocks data – to a physical robot, we address the differences between simulation and reality in three stages.

Before data generation, we perform system identification by tuning simulated robot parameters, including joint friction and armature (the motor and gearbox inertia reflected at the joint), to match real-robot trajectories. During data generation, we randomize physical properties (object size, friction, and table height) and visual properties (lighting, backgrounds, materials, and camera parameters). At inference time, observations are captured using a front-facing ZED camera and a wrist-mounted ZED Mini. For policies that use depth images, we generate clean depth maps, which estimate distance at each pixel, from paired red-green-blue (RGB) camera images using FastFoundationStereo, rather than relying on noisy depth sensor measurements.

The physical ToyBlocks setup: a robot arm, wooden blocks, and a camera.

ToyBlocks connects data generation, training, and evaluation in one controlled setting, so researchers can investigate how robots learn over time and test how changes to a model or its training data affect robot behavior. We’re releasing simulation assets, procedural task and demonstration generators, automatically generated demonstrations, two trained models showcasing what the framework can do (one based on Molmo 2 and one based on ManiFlow), training code, and evaluation code and validation sets. This allows other teams to build their own training mixtures and investigate failure modes beyond those covered in our initial experiments.

Our initial data release is a proof point with 85,336 long-horizon demonstrations, each comprising about 6–12 skill demonstrations, depending on the set. The initial datasets cover nearly 1,600 hours of robot execution data and 144 million frames. In a few weeks, we're targeting a second release with a larger-scale dataset, more skills, and more comprehensive benchmarking. We’ll also add fully integrated RL training capability that is not contained in the current package.

Other directions for ToyBlocks include bimanual (two-arm) manipulation and dexterous robot hands, equipped with force and touch sensors for studying motion and tasks that involve frequent physical contact. We're also exploring play with unstructured piles of blocks as a way to collect data and study how new behaviors and tasks might emerge through interaction.

Future direction: RL-based pile manipulation.

Future direction: bimanual block manipulation.

With ToyBlocks, we want to advance the science of robot learning toward a future where robots can reliably apply what they've learned to unfamiliar tasks and environments. We encourage the research community to explore ToyBlocks for their own investigations and even as a basis to build their own FoundationWorlds.

#9860. How to prebake pie crust — and why you should: The key to flaky — not flabby — pie crust.

A soggy bottom. Not something you want for your baby. Or your pie crust. And while we can’t help you with your baby, there’s a simple solution to pies with soggy bottoms: prebake (also known as blind bake) the crust.

There are a number of reasons your pie can end up with a soft, pale, underbaked crust — and steps you can take to help prevent that unfortunate result.

But the one surefire way to make certain your pie’s crust will be golden brown, crisp, and delicious — just as appealing as its filling — is to prebake it. That’s right: bake the bottom crust first, before adding the filling.

Most commonly, it's smart to prebake pie crust when:

But some fillings might instead cook fully on the stovetop, like the rich, thick filling for chocolate cream pie. When it’s done, you simply pour it into its crust — and said crust had better be prebaked to perfection, since the pie’s not going anywhere near an oven.

Other pies, typically those with a more delicate, egg- and cream-based filling (think custard pie or quiche) require at least some baking — but don’t spend long enough in the oven (at a high enough temperature) to guarantee a fully baked, brown and crispy crust.

In these cases, you need to prebake your crust.

The recipe you're following may explain explicitly how to prebake your crust. But if it doesn't, follow this process:

First, roll your bottom crust and place it in the pan. Crimp or flatten the edge. Chill it for 30 minutes, to relax the gluten and firm up the fat(s); this will help prevent shrinkage, so don't skip!

Line the crust with foil, parchment, or a paper coffee filter. Fill it about two-thirds full with dried beans, uncooked rice (or other uncooked grain berries), pie weights, or granulated sugar.

Bake the crust in a preheated 375°F oven for 20 minutes, set on a baking stone or steel if you have one. Remove the crust from the oven and lift out the liner and weights. (If you’ve used sugar, save it for your future baking; it’ll be lightly toasted and yummy!)

At this point your crust is partially prebaked, and good for any of your pies that tend to exhibit a wan, flabby bottom crust when done. Think pumpkin pie: You don’t want to bake the filling so long that it’s stiff and dry, but you may pull your pie out of the oven to find your perfectly baked filling is resting in a partially baked crust. Prebaking your crust partway is a sensible solution for this scenario.

To fully prebake the crust, prick the bottom all over with a fork to prevent bubbles. Return the crust to the oven and bake for an additional 20 to 25 minutes, until it’s golden all over.

If, despite your best efforts, the lined, weighted crust still slips down the inside of the pan while it prebakes, try this: Bake the crust upside down.

To start, you’ll need two identical (or nicely nestable) pie pans with flat rims.

Place your rolled-out crust in one of the pans, anchoring it to the rim of the pan with a fork-tine crimp. Place a liner of some kind (same as above: parchment, foil, coffee filter) into the pan. Nest the second pan into the first.

Pick up both pans, turn them over, and set them on a baking sheet. Place the baking sheet and pie pans in the oven, and bake as directed above. As the crust bakes, gravity will pull it down toward its rim — rather than into a puddle at the bottom of the pan. Magic!

After 20 minutes remove the baking sheet from the oven, carefully turn the pans over, lift out the empty pan, and remove the liner. At this point, your crust is partially prebaked. To prebake it fully, place the crust back in the oven, right side up, and bake until it's golden.

If you struggle with a pale, pasty bottom crust in your fruit pie, then yes, you can prebake it — with a couple of caveats:

So, soggy bottoms begone! From now on I expect every pie you bake will have a deep golden brown, flaky, crispy crust on the bottom — all because of the prebake.

And if you have any other questions about pie — from creating tender, flaky crust to thickening fruit filling to assessing when your pie is perfectly baked — please check out our Pie Baking Guide.

#9858. Container Queries and Focus Management: Building Resilient Components with TailwindCSS v4

When integrating meta/astryx into a production TypeScript stack last quarter, we hit a painful wall: our card components looked pristine in desktop viewports but collapsed into unusable layouts when nested inside sidebars or widget containers. The root cause wasn't the design system itself—it was our reliance on viewport-based media queries instead of container queries. Combined with improperly managed focus trapping in modal overlays, our accessibility score tanked.

Viewport-based breakpoints assume a global coordinate system. When meta/astryx components lived inside a max-w-xs sidebar, our md: and lg: classes fired anyway, rendering a responsive grid that had no space to breathe.

TailwindCSS v4 gives us container queries out of the box:

In your Tailwind config, container queries are enabled by default in v4. The @sm, @md, @lg prefixes correspond to container widths (640px, 768px, 1024px).

Here's a reusable card component that adapts to its container context:

The beauty: drop this component anywhere—sidebar, modal, main content—and it responds intelligently to available space.

Our second catastrophe: screen readers navigated straight through our modal overlay into the background DOM. Users with keyboard-only input couldn't escape modals without tabbing through 200 hidden elements.

Using Radix primitives (which meta/astryx often builds on), focus management becomes declarative:

Radix handles focus trap internally: Tab cycles only within the modal, Escape closes it, and screen readers announce role and title on entry.

Combine container queries with a discrete fade animation:

Tailwind's data-* selectors make this trivial:

When testing meta/astryx's component library, ensure your container context is set at the layout boundary—typically your main content wrapper. This prevents collision between the design system's internal breakpoints and your application's responsive strategy.

Container queries solve isolation beautifully, but they carry a performance cost on older browsers and complex nesting scenarios. Radix's focus management is bulletproof for accessibility compliance, yet it adds another dependency to your bundle. The trade-off: pick your battles. For component libraries like meta/astryx that ship into varied contexts, container queries are non-negotiable. For highly controlled admin dashboards, viewport breakpoints might suffice.

The question isn't which is objectively better—it's whether your integration pattern demands resilience in unknown containers or predictable, controlled layouts.

#9857. Why Robots Need Intelligence Built for the Physical World

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Robbyant’s LingBot 2.0 starts with the demands of perception and physical action to build intelligence across different robot bodies.

A chatbot can wait for another prompt. A robot may already be moving by the time its surroundings change. That difference turns embodied AI into a distinct engineering problem, where intelligence has to account for physical space and predict how an action will affect what happens next. Robbyant, an embodied AI company under Ant Group, built LingBot 2.0 around those demands from the beginning.

The system reflects a deceptively difficult question in robotics: What does an AI architecture need when its decisions have immediate physical consequences? Robbyant’s answer connects perception, environmental modeling, and execution through six models developed as parts of one embodied-native system.

A robot operating in a home or workplace receives a continuous stream of spatial information. Objects have depth and position, people move around, and the environment can change during a task. Understanding a verbal instruction covers only one piece of that process.

LingBot-Vision and LingBot-Depth 2.0 form the perception side of LingBot 2.0. They give robots information about objects and three-dimensional space that can feed into later reasoning and action. Robbyant describes this layer as “See Clearer,” reflecting the need for physical agents to understand where things are before deciding how to interact with them.

That spatial information also has to remain useful as conditions develop. A robot reaching toward an object needs intelligence capable of working with the environment it encounters at that moment.

The next part of the system addresses prediction. LingBot-Video and LingBot-World 2.0 model physical environments and how they develop over time, creating Robbyant’s “Think Deeper” layer.

This ability has particular significance for robots because movement changes the environment. Picking something up alters its position. Moving through a room creates a new spatial relationship with everything nearby. Effective reasoning involves anticipating what an action is likely to produce.

The models give developers a way to study environmental interaction alongside the perception data that informs it. That relationship is central to Robbyant’s full-stack approach: seeing and predicting supply information that execution can use.

Eventually, the robot has to move. LingBot-VLA 2.0 and LingBot-VA 2.0 handle the “Act Faster” portion of the architecture, translating information from earlier stages into physical behavior.

LingBot-VA 2.0 serves as the capstone of the system. Rather than adapting a model trained for language or entertainment purposes, Robbyant built it from scratch around the demands of embodied AI, with dynamic modeling and causal prediction incorporated into an architecture intended for environmental interaction and real-time execution.Latency becomes especially consequential here. Software generating text can spend additional time producing an answer with few physical consequences. A robot responding to movement around it operates on a different clock. Its perception and reasoning have to reach the action system quickly enough for the response to remain relevant.

Hardware creates another complication: bodies differ. A model working on one physical configuration may eventually need to control machines with different dimensions or capabilities.

Robbyant frames its goal as “building one brain for all robots.” LingBot-VLA 2.0 integrates data from 20 different configurations of robots from 17 different brands during the pre-training phase, enabling cross-embodiment capabilities. LingBot 2.0 as a whole approaches that ambition at the system level, connecting specialized capabilities so embodied intelligence can develop across different robot forms. The six-model architecture gives perception, prediction, and action defined roles within the same technical framework.

Selected models and technologies have also been released as open source, accompanied by technical reports or research papers. That gives developers and researchers material they can inspect and reuse while exploring embodied AI architectures.

The technical challenge of embodied AI begins once intelligence has to exist inside physical space. Every decision occurs amid changing surroundings, and an action can immediately create the conditions for the next one.

LingBot 2.0 treats that cycle as a foundation of robot intelligence. Its six models divide the work across seeing, understanding physical change, and executing movement while remaining connected as a full-stack system. For Robbyant, building a more general robot brain starts with understanding what happens when software has to act in the real world.

#9856. Browser cleanup and data retention are two different jobs

Posted on Nov 6 • Originally published at browseract.com • Fully Autonomous

An automation downloads a report, saves a screenshot for debugging, and closes a temporary browser session. The next run starts with an empty profile. The report and screenshot remain in the application's output directory.

That is an ordinary architecture, but it exposes an easy documentation mistake: describing a browser's temporary state as if it defined the retention policy for every artifact produced by the workflow.

This article presents an application design exercise. It does not report a deletion test, a security audit, or a run against a billing portal. BrowserAct's private stealth mode provides a fresh profile rather than reusable login state. The surrounding application must still decide what to do with its own files and records.

For repeated authenticated work, continuity may be useful. For a clean-state investigation, retained state can be exactly the variable you want to remove.

Make that choice for the task. Avoid selecting a temporary profile solely because the word private sounds appropriate. A recurring report collector that repeatedly loses its login may create more manual work without solving the problem you intended to address.

In BrowserAct, private mode is a stealth-browser configuration. It is not a general promise that every browser type, external account, and application output follows the same lifecycle.

Now list the outputs separately. A small workflow might produce:

These objects have different purposes. The file may be the requested business deliverable. The screenshot may only be needed during investigation. A retry record might remain useful after a browser session ends because it prevents duplicate work.

Closing a browser session does not define the lifecycle of those application-managed objects. Neither does starting the next session with a fresh profile.

For each output category, record who writes it, where it goes, who can access it, and which component is responsible for its eventual removal.

This is an illustrative inventory, not BrowserAct storage configuration or a recommended universal retention schedule. The right duration depends on the user's requirements and the system receiving the data.

The useful property is explicit ownership. If every component assumes another component will clean something up, an artifact can survive indefinitely even when the browser itself is disposable.

A failed export does not always require sharing the full account page or request capture with everyone investigating it.

If richer evidence is necessary, preserve it in the intended destination with the relevant access controls. A temporary browser is not a substitute for choosing that destination deliberately.

Separate two questions at the end of an attempt: did the requested output pass verification, and did the execution environment close as intended?

A cleanly closed session can still have downloaded an incomplete report. A verified file can still be associated with a browser session that the job forgot to close. Record those outcomes independently so the next operator can tell whether to recover the artifact or release resources.

For a failure, save enough information to choose the next action before ending the session. Do not describe every failure as a reason to preserve all browser state forever; decide which evidence the recovery actually needs.

A fresh profile can help isolate whether retained browser state influenced a result. It does not establish anonymity to a website, remove the website's records, or verify deletion from an external output store.

Use the browser mode to control continuity at the browser layer. Use the application's own artifact handling to control its outputs. Keeping those responsibilities explicit makes both the workflow and its documentation easier to review.

Our private browser automation guide explains the persistence trade-off. Apply that choice alongside an inventory of the files and evidence your application actually creates.

People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.

#9854. Grading a Machine That Read 51,008 Pages With No Answer Key

CTO & CPO | Enterprise AI & Big Data at National Scale

CTO & CPO | Enterprise AI & Big Data at National Scale

CTO & CPO | Enterprise AI & Big Data at National Scale

Konstantin Tsiolkovsky (1857–1935) derived the rocket equation and described the multistage rocket and the orbital station decades before anyone could build them. His personal papers are held as fond 555 of the Archive of the Russian Academy of Sciences in Moscow. The archive did the essential work years ago: it scanned the fond and put the images online. What it did not provide was a catalogue you can query, full-text search or a dataset. To find anything, you click through page views one file at a time.

Over the summer I built the missing layer: a catalogue of all 2,019 files, a dating for 1,969 of them taken from the archive's own catalogue cards, a classification of every page as handwriting or typescript, and a machine transcription of every page. All of it is public: a full-fond search, the dataset with a permanent DOI (10.5281/zenodo.21705221), the code and the preprint.

One caveat belongs at the top. The machine read everything and no human has verified a single page. The corpus is a finding aid, not a scholarly edition, and every file links back to the archive's own scan, which remains the source of record.

Three things about the archive's portal only became visible once I tried to use it as a data source.

The identifier in a page address is not the archival file number. Id 300 is file 297, because 31 files carry lettered numbers (145a, 585a and others) that take a position in the running sequence without advancing the archival count. A catalogue built on the obvious reading of the URLs would cite the wrong files.

The inventory number in the address is decorative. Two URLs that differ only in that number return the same document. The real archival address appears only inside the file paths of the scans.

Large scans, above roughly 800 KB, are served cut off at about 130 KB. A browser saves the stub silently with no error. The only way to get them whole was byte-range requests.

None of this is a complaint about the archive, which scanned and published 51,008 pages. It shows the distance between images on the internet and a collection you can ask questions of.

To measure recognition accuracy you need ground truth: the same text keyed in by a person. For an archival fond there is none. If there were, machine reading would be unnecessary.

The usual workaround is to lean on the model's own confidence. It does not work here, and I doubt it works anywhere that matters. A fluent invention satisfies a confidence score as well as a correct reading does. On century-old handwriting, fluent invention is exactly the failure you are worried about.

Personal archives of the typewriter era often keep one text twice: the author's manuscript and a typescript copy made from it, filed together. I read both with the same pipeline and compare the two transcriptions. The text is the same and the pipeline is the same. The only variable left is how legible the page is, so the disagreement between the two readings measures the difficulty of the handwriting.

Fond 555 holds 1,759 such pairs across 224 files. At the median, the two readings agree on 37% of the words. The median longest run they share verbatim is 10 words, and in 43% of pairs no shared run is longer. That is what "machine-read early twentieth-century manuscript" honestly means.

A proxy metric needs its own validation, and here that was possible in a small corner of the fond: files whose text also survives in a printed edition. On those, the paired-reading estimate is unbiased to within a percentage point of the true error. It also ranks pages by difficulty the way the truth does: a rank correlation of 0.67 across all 55 available pairs, 0.92 on the 32 pairs where the printed edition is demonstrably the same text, and 0.97 on the 17 most certain.

Scored directly against published editions, the transcription reaches 98.1% character accuracy on typescript and 81.1% on handwriting, or 91.7% and 73.7% at word level. Those two figures need a precise label. They were measured on the part of the corpus read by the earlier pipeline. The rest of the fond was read later by a different model and has not been scored against editions. What was measured across both parts is the paired agreement, and it is the same for both. That supports "the newer part reads no worse than the older one". It does not support "81% across the whole fond", and I do not claim it.

This is the rule I would carry into any production system. You almost never have ground truth for everything, but you almost always have it for something. Use that small piece to calibrate a proxy, check that the proxy ranks cases the way the truth does, and only then scale it.

Each of these first looked like a success.

Comparing the author's drafts turned out to be impossible. The fond holds Tsiolkovsky's "The Spaceship" in two variants, ideal material for studying how he revised it, and part of the reason I started. The two variants share 19% of their words. That is below the 37% at which two machine readings of one and the same page agree. Below the noise floor, authorial revision cannot be told apart from reading error. I closed that line of work and built the limit into the tool: the comparison script refuses to report differences that do not clear the measured threshold.

The page classifier passed its test and was still wrong. I separated handwriting from typescript by the variation in ink-stroke lengths along a line. On 19 hand-labelled pages it scored 19 out of 19. Later an independent signal appeared on 4,675 transcribed pages, and against it the classifier is 80% accurate, where always guessing the commoner class gives 54%. Carbon copies and faded typescript read as handwriting. A small, clean test set certifies a demo, not a system.

A model defect posed as data. On 236 pages the model looped and repeated one line of markup, 635 times at worst. Each repeat counted as an uncertainty mark and inflated the published total by 6,189. No statistical check caught it, because 236 pages out of 51,008 do not move any distribution. A person opening a file and looking at it did. The runs are now folded, each with a note on the page saying so, and the corpus carries 299,939 uncertainty marks, about six per scan.

The difference between a measurement and an impression is that a measurement can tell you that you were wrong. Publishing those corrections is what makes the surviving numbers worth trusting.

Newer models enable reasoning by default, and it draws on the same output budget as the answer. With a 4,096-token limit, up to 3,929 tokens went to reasoning. The transcription broke off mid-page, and the stub was indistinguishable from a poor reading. With reasoning set to minimum, quality did not drop and output volume halved.

If your pipeline evaluates model outputs, a silent truncation upstream will present itself as a quality problem downstream. Check the finish reason before you check the text.

A related edge case: two pages could not be read by any model. They are a German typewritten review of a 1927 Tsiolkovsky pamphlet, and they trip the built-in filter against reproducing known printed text verbatim. They were read by a separate route and are flagged in the corpus.

I compared candidate models on the same handwritten pages, scored against the typed copy of the same text, with the existing pipeline as the baseline. On typical handwriting no model clearly outran the rest. On a 48-page sample the more expensive model was better on 37 pages and worse on 11. The edge is real but modest, because the ceiling is set by the material, not the model.

The remaining 41,212 pages were read overnight in one batch run, for about $39. The bottleneck in work like this stopped being compute some time ago. It is measurement.

My previous post, The Model Was Never the Bottleneck, ended in the same place from the other side: the work that decides whether an AI system can be trusted is rarely the model itself.

Author’s note: This is an independent project. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by the Archive of the Russian Academy of Sciences. The method is described in a preprint (arXiv:2608.03617); the data are released under CC0 and the code under MIT.

#9853. Designing an emergency medical card: what a stranger should see when you can't consent

Picture the worst case: someone is found unconscious after a car crash. Their phone is in their pocket. The paramedic has seconds, not minutes, and the person can't answer a single question.

What should a stranger be able to see in that moment, without the person's consent, because consent is impossible?

We've been designing the emergency card for Anpheros around that question. Here are the decisions we made, the trade-offs we argued about, and the standards that make the result readable by systems that aren't ours.

The tempting answer is "everything, it's an emergency". We decided the opposite.

When the card's QR code is scanned, the page shows only the basics a first responder can act on:

That's it. There is no emergency "break-glass" access to the full history. No past diagnoses, no lab results, no notes.

Full history access goes through a different path: a clinician requests it, and the patient approves it once they can, per scope and per duration.

Medications were the one item we went back and forth on.

A full medication list is long, and some of it is sensitive (psychiatric medication, HIV treatment, hormone therapy). But some classes matter enormously in an emergency: anticoagulants, insulin, corticosteroids, antiepileptics, immunosuppressants.

Because we store medications with ATC codes, one option is to filter automatically and show only the high-risk classes on the public page. The other is to show the list the person chose to put on their card. There's no perfect answer. Whatever you choose, make it the person's decision, made in advance, with a preview of exactly what a stranger will see.

A tourist collapses in Lisbon; the paramedic reads Portuguese. A card written in English free text helps a little. A card in Polish doesn't help at all.

The fix isn't translation at scan time. It's storing coded data from the start:

Then the emergency page renders the labels in the reader's language. Coded data translates cleanly; free text like "allergic to the pink antibiotic" never will.

The emergency subset maps almost one-to-one onto the International Patient Summary (IPS): allergies and intolerances, medication summary, immunizations, problems. Using IPS means any IPS-aware system can read the same data, not just our app.

For moving it around, SMART Health Links are designed for exactly this: a link, often in a QR code, that resolves to encrypted FHIR data, with an optional expiry and passcode.

If you build your own format, you've built a card that only your app can read. That's the opposite of what an emergency card is for.

Putting the card in the phone's Wallet, next to boarding passes, is the obvious UX choice. But the two platforms work very differently:

For health data in the EU (a special category under GDPR Article 9), that difference matters. Our rule: the Wallet pass carries only the minimum (name, date of birth, blood group and the QR code), and everything else stays on our servers behind the QR. If you need to change what's shown, you change it in one place.

If you read what paramedics say about phone medical IDs, the pattern is consistent: locked phones, every brand hides the info somewhere different, and there's rarely time to look. A bracelet or a wallet card gets checked because it's visible.

So we treat the digital card as a complement. If someone has a serious allergy, epilepsy, diabetes or takes anticoagulants, a physical bracelet is still the first thing a responder will see.

I'm the founder of Anpheros, a patient-owned health record built on FHIR R4 and IPS, so these are decisions we live with. If you're building something similar, I'd love to hear where you landed, especially on the medications question.

#9851. Forget Takeout: Customers Love These Frozen Mexican Foods

If you're lucky, you live just a short ride away from a half dozen quality Mexican restaurants serving bubbling bowls of pozole, punchy tacos, and sultry stews of slow-cooked meats. But not everyone lives in communities blessed with quality Mexican cooking. And that's a major bummer, because this regional cuisine is simply electric, balancing deep flavors with fresh herbs, warm spices, and piquant chiles. Mexican food plays with different textures and shapes, allowing you to compose bites that are simultaneously creamy and crisp, cool and spicy, savory and sweet.

Thankfully, you can enjoy decent Mexican and Tex-Mex-inspired food from the comfort of your couch. And all it takes is a trip to your local supermarket. First, let's preface this entire article by saying that a good restaurant will almost always outdo a frozen dupe. Still, there is something to be said for the convenience and cost savings of air-frying a chimichanga or microwaving a burrito for lunch. I turned to the internet to find frozen Mexican meals comparable to what you might get at a restaurant or fast-casual takeout spot. After sorting through hundreds of reviews and comments, I put together a list of the top customer-favorite Mexican appetizers, sides, and main meals available in the freezer aisle.

The foundation of a good tamale is corn, specifically corn that's been soaked in an alkaline solution (AKA nixtamalized), which transforms the dense starchy kernels into a pliable, dough-like carbohydrate called masa. Making masa (and tamales) requires time, skill, precision, and technique. But if you don't possess any of the above, then heating up a frozen tamale is your best option.

There are a surprising number of choices in this department, but customers are especially fond of the Trader Joe's versions. Like many Trader Joe's items, people gripe that these come in and out of stock with about as much predictability as a June weather forecast. However, the cheese and green chile and the chicken and cheese varieties are consistently the most reliable (and available). Tamales make a good side dish, especially if you want an alternative to potatoes or pasta, or, like one Redditor, you can steam one and bring it for lunch. A negative is that since they have to be reheated, the masa interior can get a tad dry. To remedy this, Trader Joe's shoppers recommend a side of salsa, hot sauce, guacamole, rice and beans, or a blanket of extra melted cheese.

As far as frozen Mexican entrées go, the burrito bowl can be controversial. Why? Unlike a tamale, chimichanga, or taquito, a burrito bowl doesn't require the same finesse, so customers generally expect a higher quality product. Surprisingly, many reliable brands struggle to execute what seems like a simple dish. But not Kevin's Natural Foods. If unfamiliar, Kevin's positions itself as a better-for-you frozen meal. Ingredients are clean, non-GMO, and gluten-free. These restrictions are far from a hindrance. On the contrary, the quality of Kevin's frozen meals, especially its burrito bowls, is top-notch.

At least, that's what the customers say. "Absolutely loaded with cheese, chicken in every bite, rice perfectly cooked, veggies still have a bit of a snap to them, and the chipotle sauce has a ton of flavor," one Redditor commented. Others shared a similar opinion. With Kevin's, there's a general appreciation for the quality and portion size. The brand doesn't skimp on proteins or portion size, and whatever ingredients are included are thoughtfully prepared — no mushy rice, sad veggies, or gloopy cheese. The result keeps customers happy.

Many culinary historians consider mole the national dish of Mexico. The sauce's dynamic flavors mirror the country's history: dark and complex, with an underlying sweetness and grounding depth. Mole requires dozens of Mexico's most prized indigenous ingredients — chocolate, chiles, nuts, seeds, spices — to create something that's, frankly, unmatched in any other cuisine.

Does Trader Joe's version capture that centuries of Mexican culinary tradition? That would be impossible. However, given its price and unbelievable convenience, it does a pretty good job of imitating the sweet-and-savory balance of a traditional mole. With just one package, you can make multiple meals. And while a traditional mole takes hours — if not days — to prepare, TJ's frozen chicken mole takes just minutes in the microwave.

The taste is bold, but the texture of the chicken — not overly mushy or stringy — makes it ideal for several applications. Customers say they use it to fill enchiladas and tacos, but you can use it for everything from pizza to nachos to an omelet.

Known for its better-for-you ingredient profile, Amy's has been supplying organic frozen entrées for decades. While some frozen tortilla-wrapped items suffer from a textural breakdown, the tortillas housing Amy's enchilada filling hold up well. All of Amy's frozen entrées are vegetarian-friendly, but where they lack in meat, they make up for it in texture, flavor, and composition. Amy's cheese enchiladas have been a hit with shoppers for decades, with the blend of cheeses, toasty corn tortillas, and savory tomato-based enchilada sauce, and they still earn online praise today.

"I find these to have an incredible depth of flavor for a frozen meal," began one Redditor's review. "I would be 100% happy if this was served to me in a restaurant." Others say that the product is the best in frozen food. And while there's no question that shoppers have enjoyed and appreciated the taste of Amy's foods for years, they are a bit disgruntled about the ever-increasing price point. And while that might be on the higher end of the price spectrum, anything in the $7 or $8 range for a frozen meal does seem a little steep. But they're still beloved, despite that.

The taquito was created as a thrifty way to use up leftover tortillas and filling. Little did its creators know that the fried, toasty snack would become widely beloved happy marriage of taste, form, and texture. Taquitos are almost always made from corn tortillas and filled with everything from chicken and cheese to beef, veggies, and beans. But the best part of a taquito is its tubular shape that's seemingly designed for dipping.

Frozen taquitos aren't new, and their basic composition hasn't changed much over the years. You'll find a plethora of options in the freezer aisle, but customers are most fond of El Monterey's Extra Crunchy Southwest Chicken variety. Fans say it's hard to eat just one... or two. Shoppers also love its unique exterior crust.

The only downside to El Monterey's taquitos is the quantity of filling. There's a collective sigh at how the interiors have grown increasingly barren over the years, an observation noticeable in the chicken taquitos, where the chicken and vegetables retain their individual shapes, unlike the beef and bean option, which is more of a paste. An easy solution is to prepare a few different dips — sour cream, guacamole, queso — to add extra moisture and unctuousness.

If a taquito and a burrito had a baby, it would be a chimichanga. It's deep-fried, which ups the richness but also gives the tortilla a crispy shell that's the ideal foil for any smooth refried bean or cheese filling. Deep frying at home doesn't require the same precision as making a chocolate soufflé, but it still means more work and cleanup than simply reheating on a hot frying pan. That's why a good frozen chimichanga is crucial if you suddenly get that itch for this fried Tex-Mex specialty. And, again, the El Monterey brand delivers.

Online, there was a lot of love for El Monterey, saying it has some of the best frozen burritos and chimichangas on the market. Unlike the taquitos, the chimichangas have a generous filling that, as one person put it, is comparable to the reference photo on the bag. The key to executing these properly is in the preparation. The chimichanga is inherently greasy, so a quick thaw in the microwave followed by a crisp-up on a hot pan usually does the trick. An air-fryer works, too. Some people just throw them in the deep fryer because, well, why not?

The burrito is the quintessential frozen Mexican food item, and over the decades, dozens — if not hundreds — of brands have battled each other for category supremacy. Many have faltered, but a handful have held their ground. Like Red's. Founded in 2009, Red's focuses on one thing: burritos. Sure, it'll try a breakfast sandwich or a "Snacker," but its product lineup is mostly just an array of tortilla-wrapped goodies.

Customers are big fans of the steak and cheddar burrito. While other cheaper, mass-market frozen burritos rely on mushy, indistinguishable fillings, Red's has made a name for itself by using higher-quality ingredients. Although shoppers are big fans of Red's entire line of burritos, they do gripe about the prices. Heating the burrito is another issue entirely, but one Red's expert has a foolproof method: Run it under water in the sink for a few seconds before microwaving. The extra moisture makes the tortilla a bit springier and more pliable. Wrapping it in a wet paper towel will have a similar effect.

The Mexican Style Street Corn Triangles from Tastiez are far from traditional Mexican cuisine. Instead, they are a frozen food product inspired by the classic Mexican street food esquites, which is like a bolder, saltier version of creamed corn. Another way to think of it is like elote, that yummy, cheese-dusted ear of grilled corn, stripped off the cob.

This product is a major departure from the original dish, but if you're craving an easy appetizer inspired by an authentic Mexican dish, it's not such a bad substitute. And, most importantly (at least for this article), customers have given these fried, corn-filled triangles their seal of approval. Whereas your average stuffed, fried snack oozes its insides after a hard bake or big bite, these stay pretty much intact. The crisp outside and gooey center make for a satisfying finger food, but it's the taste that brings it home, with reviewers gushing over its delicious street corn flavor. They come out best when deep-fried, but the air-fryer is an excellent alternative that still yields a crisp exterior.

Today, you can find the most elaborate culinary delights in your supermarket freezer. But while brands can execute everything from frozen kimbap to cioppino, many still struggle to nail a good frozen taco. What has customers complaining is the ratio of filling to shell: not enough of the former and too much of the latter, resulting in a product that's dry and brittle. Maybe tacos are difficult to seal, so manufacturers are forced to under fill? Whatever the reason, some brands miss the mark, while others, like Don Miguel, lead by example.

The Don Miguel Chicken Chipotle Mini Tacos have an active and passionate Reddit community that few items on this list can match. But why? What makes this 50-pack of frozen tacos from Costco so special? The price and crave-worthiness. However, while the consensus is generally positive, long-time customers have commented that the tacos are a bit spicier than they used to be. For this issue, the main workaround is a cooling condiment, like Greek yogurt or sour cream. Still, although people do love these things, it seems like the perfect mini taco has yet to be discovered.

The churro is one of the most globally recognized Mexican desserts. It's basically a twist or extruded wand of fried dough that's tossed in cinnamon sugar and served with, if you're lucky, a smooth chocolate sauce or caramel. Churros come in many shapes and sizes. Costco, famous for scaling everything to the max, sells a foot-long version in its food court for just $1.49. But if you want to scratch that churro itch at home, you can pick up a pack of Hola Churros.

No, these aren't as long as the ones you'll find in the food court, but some regular Costco customers think they're just smaller versions of the same make and model. But how do they taste? Overall, shoppers are pretty pleased. Are they as crisp and pleasantly oily as the ones you'll find at a street fair or Mexican restaurant? Probably not. But they do the job. The key is finding ways to deliver that extra punch of flavor. Although they come with individual packs of cinnamon sugar, some Redditors recommend drizzling chocolate on them. They're also good as a topping for an ice cream sundae. For heating, skip the microwave and go for the air-fryer or toaster oven. No matter how you make them, they are an unbelievably good value: around $14.49 for a box of 30.

When you see a chile relleno on the menu at a Mexican restaurant, it's worth getting. This dish is pretty special, integrating all the different tastes and flavors that make cuisine from this part of the world so interesting and seductive. It's essentially a cheese-stuffed pepper that's battered, fried, and served on top of a rich tomato sauce. It takes some work to prepare, but it's a real stunner when it hits the table.

Somehow the team at Trader Joe's has managed to capture all these dynamic tastes and textures in one convenient, easy-to-heat frozen package. The batter is tempura-style, somewhat spongy but not in a soggy way, providing heft and unctuousness to the otherwise bare, roasted pepper wrapper. The cheese is pleasantly rubbery, and the sauce is savory and delicious. On Reddit, customers are surprised by how good it tastes, even despite the soft, slightly mushy texture. Of all the foods on this list, this one had the most overwhelmingly positive score for flavor. The consensus is that you should reheat the peppers in the air-fryer, not the microwave. Overall, people think the flavor is fantastic, and for just $5.99, you really can't go wrong.

Although this brand of Trader Joe's frozen rice is called "Spanish-style," its flavor profile is decidedly Mexican, drawing on spices and ingredients indigenous to Central America. Tomato gives it its mellow orange color, and a savory spice blend and quick toasting add an umami undertone that makes it easy to pair with dishes from across the culinary landscape, from madras lentils to gyros.

On Reddit, Trader Joe's faithful say it's an excellent accompaniment to many of the store's frozen and refrigerated Mexican entrées, like the birria, mole, green chili and cheese tamales, and even the salad kits. Others use it as a quick and flavorful foundation to a dish. Its utility is what makes this product so special. With dozens of comments on one Reddit thread dedicated to the Spanish-style rice, you can find dozens of interesting and inventive use cases. And while it's marketed as a microwavable grain, some shoppers are convinced you get a better result when you toast it in a pan.

First, I identified some of the more popular Mexican dishes that come frozen. From there, I explored different brands, and using Reddit, Facebook, and other social media channels, I got a sense of which products performed best.

For example, the top taquito maker didn't necessarily deliver the best burrito. I wanted to present a variety, so I didn't repeat dishes. It was difficult to find the top flavor(s), so when there wasn't a clear consensus, I tended to go with the one with the most feedback and attention.

#9850. How long does pie last in the fridge? : Because we're all wondering what to do with our apple and pumpkin pies.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions. Today: How long does pie last in the fridge?

The season of plentiful pies is upon us. When preparing several pies for a holiday meal, you may be wondering about the imminent leftovers. Should apple pie be stored differently than pumpkin pie? David from our Baker’s Hotline is here with his expert advice to help.

“Baked apple or other fruit pies can be kept covered, at room temperature, for one to two days. After that, they’ll keep in the fridge for one to two more days,” David advises. A 15-minute reheat in a 350°F oven can help revive some of that freshly baked flavor. Tent the pie with foil so it doesn’t brown further.

Interested in prepping ahead? David says that storing an assembled, ready-to-bake apple pie is a bad idea; the fruity filling will release moisture, which will make your crust soggy. Instead, roll out your pie crusts and prep your apples, but keep them separate. And wait to add the sugar and spices to the apples until you’re ready to bake the pie. This way, you can pour off any liquid that’s accumulated from the fruit without draining off your thickener, sugar, and spices.

Sliced apples turn brown, so you don’t want to keep your prepared apples in the fridge very long before baking. Aim for under 24 hours, but a squeeze of lemon juice could help them last another day or so.

And if you want to use your freezer to prep ahead, here’s how to freeze and bake fruit pies.

David advises, “Baked pumpkin pie or other pies containing eggs and/or dairy such as pecan pie, custard pie, or chiffon pie should be stored refrigerated; they’ll keep in the fridge for three to four days. I like to transfer the pie to a shallow, lidded storage container, but plastic wrap or a storage top can be used as well.”

As with apple, if you’re making your pumpkin (and other custard) pie ahead, it’s best to keep filling and crust separate. Pumpkin pie filling can be made ahead; it’ll keep, refrigerated, overnight. In fact, that's actually what we recommend doing; the custard develops incredible flavor and aroma as it sits.

If you can, serve pies the day they were made instead of refrigerating them.

Reheat refrigerated pies in a 350°F oven for about 15 minutes prior to serving.

Apple and other fruit pies will last at room temperature for up to two days, then in the fridge for two more.

Pumpkin, custard, or other egg/dairy-based pies can be stored in the fridge for up to four days.

If you’re making the crust and the filling ahead, keep them separated until it’s time to bake your pie.

#9848. How to Generate, Recalculate, and Validate Excel Workbooks With Python

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

The fastest way to lose a finance team is to send them a number they can't click on.

A dashboard shows a total. Finance wants to see how the total was built: which rows, which filter, which formula. If they can't see it, they export the data and rebuild it in Excel, and now there are two numbers and a meeting about why they differ.

So a lot of what I automate for finance ships as a workbook. The detail rows sit on one sheet. The summary cells are formulas that point at them. Click a customer's revenue and you see =SUMIFS(detail!$D$2:$D$7,detail!$B$2:$B$7,A2). Anyone can audit it in the tool they already trust, without asking me a thing.

Generating those workbooks from Python is easy. Generating them so they're actually right takes a few extra steps that nobody mentions until something breaks.

openpyxl writes any string that starts with = as a formula. Here's a small revenue workbook: invoices on a detail sheet, and a summary sheet with one SUMIFS per customer, a total, and a check row.

The check row subtracts the detail total from the summary total. It should always be zero. It's there for the reviewer, and as you'll see, for the code.

Open that file in Excel and every formula calculates. Read it with anything else and the formulas have no values:

pandas does the same thing. A total row written as a formula reads as NaN:

An xlsx file stores two things for each formula cell: the formula, and the value from the last time it was calculated. openpyxl has no calculation engine, so it writes the first and not the second. Anything that reads values without recalculating, including pandas and the next script in your pipeline, sees nothing.

LibreOffice can open the file without a window, calculate every formula, and save it back with the values stored:

After that, data_only=True returns 4335.75 for the total, and the formula is still there for the reviewer. Wrapped in Python:

Two details in that function exist because of the next gotcha.

If you build several workbooks, the obvious move is to recalculate them in parallel. Here's what happened when I converted six files at the same time with LibreOffice's default settings:

Six processes. Six exit codes of zero. Five files. I ran it again and got the same result.

By default, every LibreOffice process uses the same user profile, and a second soffice that starts while another is running tries to hand its request to the one already running. You can see it in the logs: conversion messages turn up in the wrong process's output. Most requests get done. Sometimes one doesn't, and nothing in the exit code tells you.

Write =XLOOKUP("b",A2:A3,B2:B3) with openpyxl and Excel shows #NAME?. So does LibreOffice, which tells you it isn't an Excel quirk:

Functions added to Excel after the original file format, such as XLOOKUP, IFS, CONCAT, and TEXTJOIN, are stored in the file with an _xlfn. prefix. Excel adds the prefix when you type the formula. openpyxl doesn't, so you have to.

The workbook exists and the formulas calculate. Are they right? A SUMIFS whose range stops one row short is a perfectly valid formula. So after recalculating, read the values back and compare them with the same totals computed in pandas:

If any customer is off by more than half a cent, or the check cell isn't zero, the script raises and the workbook doesn't go out. That's the real job of the check row: a reviewer can see it, and the code can enforce it.

Dashboards are good at "what's happening?" Workbooks are good at "show me." Finance asks the second question far more often, especially at month end, and especially about the numbers that move money.

A workbook with live formulas answers it without a meeting. It also makes your work auditable by the people whose job is auditing, which is the fastest way I know to get them to trust a number they didn't build.
