#9794. 10 Best Chain Italian Subs, According To Customer Reviews

The Italian sub is its own category of cuisine. Born of the ingenuity of Italian immigrants, this centuries-old sandwich balances the highest forms of culinary technique with the simplest combination of ingredients. Expertly cured meats, creamy provolone cheese, crisp vegetables, and the right formula of oil and vinegar — all layered on a crusty roll, hoagie, or baguette — meld into a perfectly harmonious bite that's simultaneously salty, tangy, punchy, and fresh. Within this basic framework is room for limitless personalization. Some shops adorn their Italian sandwich with mayonnaise or hot relish. Another might add prosciutto or smoked ham or a stack of vinegary banana peppers. One may even toast the thing.

That's why the Italian sub is such a fun food to explore. No two are identical — even if they use exactly the same ingredients. Obviously, a sandwich with so much history is an easy target for dissection and judgment. Customers have their favorites, especially when it comes to what's offered at popular chain restaurants. And they're not afraid to share their feelings. For this article, I looked through hundreds of reviews, comments, and posts to find the Italian sub sandwiches with the highest customer ratings and feedback. The chains on this list range from dedicated sandwich spots to supermarkets to gas–station chains, but they all put together a great Italian sub.

With higher-quality ingredients, sliced-to-order meats, and lettuce shredded so thin it defies Newtonian mechanics, you could argue Jersey Mike's has successfully redefined the fast-casual sub. But a sandwich shop — especially one with the word "Jersey" in its name — is really only as good as its Italian sub. And in this department, Mike's Original Italian (AKA "The #13") delivers. It's a classic "Jersey-style" Italian sandwich, filled with provolone, ham, prosciuttini, capicola, salami, and pepperoni, creating a symphony of sweet, spicy, and savory meats.

"I went to Jersey Mike's for the first time and had one of the best subs I've had in a long time – #13 Italian sub done Mike's way," starts one Reddit thread. "13, Mike's way, add relish is the best Italian sandwich I have had since buying them from Italian bakeries as a kid." noted another commenter. The overall consensus is that Jersey Mike's takes pride in its product, and that getting the sandwich "Mike's Way," with a topping of tomato, onion, olive oil, red wine vinegar, oregano, and salt, elevates the experience to what you may find at a local Italian deli. It seems the community has spoken: Jersey Mike's is the best.

With over 2,500 locations across the country, Jimmy John's is one of the largest sandwich chains in the U.S., and while not all its sandwiches receive universal praise, one exception stands out: the JJ's Italian Night Club. And just like its major competitor, Jersey Mike's, Jimmy John's doesn't reinvent the wheel with its Italian sandwich. It's a classic combination of meat (salami, capicola, ham), provolone cheese, onion, lettuce, tomato, mayo, oil, vinegar, and seasonings, all served on freshly baked French bread.

Customers love the bread at Jimmy John's — just not its appearance. "Their bread looks plain AF, but it really do hit," said one Redditor. "That bread looks sad, but the Italian night club with hot peppers is the only sandwich that gets my money there," mentioned another. To deal with this boring bread, regulars recommend toasting it to achieve a light-brown crust and accentuate its yeasty aroma. The aforementioned hot peppers are another game changer, adding a tart, vinegary bite and lingering heat that cuts through the otherwise rich and meaty sandwich. One insider suggests that, when ordering the hot peppers, ask for extra.

While Jersey Mike's and Jimmy John's have thousands of locations scattered throughout the country, there are a handful of smaller regional chains serving quality, thoughtfully assembled sub sandwiches. Penn Station is one of them. With over 300 restaurants across the South and Midwest, Penn Station is winning over the hearts (and stomachs) of its customers with a concentrated menu of subs, wraps, hand-crafted sandwiches, and seasonal specials. As with most sub chains, its Classic Grilled Italian is getting the most attention. Along with the typical ingredient lineup, Penn Station uses smoked ham and banana peppers, minor tweaks that add a little electricity to its signature sandwich.

On Reddit, the sandwich receives gushing adoration from regular customers. "Penn Station's Italian sub has a hold on me," starts one thread. A lot of the love has to do with the mayonnaise, which one person described as "otherworldly." But what makes up the bulk of every sub sandwich is its bread, and here, again, Penn Station doesn't falter, with several customers noting its flavor and texture as a main contributor to the chain's overall success.

DiBella's began as a neighborhood grocery store in upstate New York around a hundred years ago. A lot has changed in the centuries since, just not the quality of its sandwiches, which have remained undeniably delicious for decades. Now, I know that we've talked a lot about bread already, but DiBella's might produce the best loaf of the bunch. The dough is aged for a minimum of 16 hours, scored by hand, and baked fresh two times a day to ensure customers never bite into something even remotely stale, which is why one enthusiastic customer called it the GOAT.

Online, people are impressed that the chain can execute mom-and-pop level taste and freshness (and an impeccable meatball sub). "DiBella's is amazing...It's hard to believe it's a chain," noted a fan. But how's the sandwich itself? Well, with a name like DiBella's, you know that its signature sandwich, aptly named "The Godfather" delivers everything you could want in a good Italian sub. All in all, it's a very solid sandwich that needs to be on your radar.

Cheba Hut's branding reads like something from a college dorm room, but its food quality is anything but juvenile or half-baked. Across the board, Cheba Hut does solid sandwiches, but its La Canna has emerged as a fan favorite, with one thread titled "My New Favorite Sub," getting over 100 upvotes on Reddit.

The La Canna distinguishes itself from other Italian subs by using prosciutto in place of the more common capicola, along with Genoa salami and smoked ham. Equally important is the ingredient balance, which pairs crisp vegetables, meat, and cheese with a tangy "shake & house" dressing. "Can't beat a La Canna on garlic herb," said one Redditor. But what makes Cheba Hut so special is its general culture of sandwich lawlessness. There are few rules here; you can get your sandwiches with alfalfa sprouts or cream cheese, on garlic bread, or served alongside a bowl of French onion soup for dipping.

Potbelly doesn't get the respect it deserves. While most of the chains on this list specialize in sandwiches, Potbelly does it all: wraps, salads, soups, subs, chili, milkshakes, mac and cheese, and one of the best club sandwiches around. But with so much variety, it's easy to be fooled into thinking it's a "jack of all trades, master of none" scenario, but this isn't the case at all.

But the Italian sandwich, although slightly more conservative than its other sandwich offering, is still tasty and reliable. Unlike other chains, Potbelly offers four — not three — heavy-hitting meats, including salami, old-world capicola, pepperoni, and mortadella — a detail that only the most observant sandwich snobs appreciate. "Their Italian is the best chain sub shop Italian out there. Nowhere else has mortadella," noted a Redditor. Others appreciate the sandwich, as well, with one person saying it's their "top choice for a commercial chain place." But what really sets this sandwich apart from the others is the giardiniera, a quintessential Chicago topping of hot pickled peppers, carrots, celery, and other veggies. The condiment is so desirable that Potbelly even sells it by the jar.

Unlike some of the other sandwich chains on this list, PrimoHoagies specializes in Italian subs. And that distinction, especially for a Philadelphia-based operation, leaves little room for error. PrimoHoagies is so committed to the Italian sandwich that it offers not one, not two, but five different variations, each with a different formula of sweet, spicy, and sharp meats and cheeses. Online, the sandwiches at PrimoHoagie's are both widely celebrated and the source of debate, specifically for the quantity of meat packed between its bread.

But many customers think this is a good problem and actually appreciate the quantity and value. In many ways, this is the most authentic sandwich of the bunch. It doesn't come with bells and whistles, just a short list of quality ingredients layered on an "award-winning seeded bread." And if you really have an issue with the quantity of cold cuts, just ask the sandwich makers for some extra veggies.

No one thinks twice about grabbing groceries at a supermarket, but for whatever reason, when it comes to prepared foods — especially sandwiches — shoppers are a little more hesitant. But when you really think about it, the supermarket, with its endless inventory of fresh vegetables, breads, meats, and cheeses, is the ideal place to grab a sub. Publix, a chain of grocery stores popular in Florida and the Southern United States, has made a name for itself in the sandwich department. Whereas other supermarkets haphazardly throw their sandwiches together, Publix constructs its subs with care and attention.

Online, customers voice their appreciation. "There are few things better in life than a Pub Sub," mentioned a Redditor. And despite being a regional supermarket chain, Publix has legions of followers across the country who will make a special trip whenever they're nearby. The supermarket's Italian sub, which comes with the classic trio of meats and provolone, isn't revolutionary, but what sets the sandwich apart is the quality of the vegetables and freshly-baked Italian Five Grain sub roll. Add some oil and vinegar for a perfectly balanced bite.

Wawa has a cult following, and for good reason. Its to-go meals, subs, sides, and secret off-menu items are terrific, even compared to fast-casual chains dedicated specifically to the craft of sandwich making. If you're unfamiliar with Wawa, you can order via a handy touchpad, where you can order sandwiches as-is or customize them to your preferences. If you suffer from choice paralysis, its predesigned subs are a terrific option. One that constantly scores high marks is its Italian sub.

In a ranking of all the Wawa subs (or hoagies if you're from Philadelphia), The Takeout declared the Italian the best option, citing its flavorful collection of meats and deft blend of salty, spicy, and fresh ingredients. This is far from a fluke. One Reddit thread dedicated to Wawa's Italian Sub has over 400 upvotes, with users describing their specific orders in the comments. Some people go standard, but many regulars like to add extra meat and cheese, jalapeños, oil and vinegar, or garlic aioli. But it's the entire Wawa experience that has won over the hearts of its customers. You can fill up your gas tank, grab a quick sandwich, and be back on the road in just a few minutes.

Another gas station moonlighting as a fast-casual stop for quality grub, QuickChek isn't so different from Wawa. And the same goes for the quality of its subs. Both chains offer a similar digital ordering platform where customers can choose every aspect of their sandwich, from the toppings to the bread. Sub sandwiches shouldn't leave you hungry, and QuickChek is a bang for your buck. But don't take our word for it. In 2021, QuickChek was named the "Best Value" for Italian subs in New Jersey, according to New Jersey Monthly.

And when you see some of its sandwiches, you'll know why. One of its Signature Subs, the Giant Italian, lives up to its name: a mammoth foot-long sub loaded with ham, salami, pepperoni, fresh mozzarella, tomato, onion, lettuce, garlic aioli, and a dynamite cherry pepper relish. On Facebook, regulars agree that for the price, speed, and accessibility, it's hard to beat a QuickChek sandwich. It's all love for this affordable convenience chain.

I used Reddit, Facebook, roundups, and other social media channels to identify the best Italian subs from popular chains. Some were obvious, but others surprised me. I kept it to chains with more than 50 locations.

If a supermarket or gas station/QSR hybrid reportedly puts together consistently good subs, it made the list. You'll notice a couple of the big names were excluded, and that's due to the fact that it seems that the quality has slipped so low that the general consensus amongst consumers, especially ones knowledgeable/passionate enough to discuss sandwiches on message boards, was unfavorable.

#9790. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

#9787. Make Your Scrambled Eggs Cracker Barrel-Style With This Easy Method (No Butter Required)

Cracker Barrel's best-selling menu item is a classic pancake, bacon, and egg combo, and no small part of that is because of the eggs. But according to a self-identified employee on Reddit, the old-timey establishment achieves such a delicious breakfast by keeping things simple, cooking them on a griddle with just canola oil — no butter.

When you include abundant fat in scrambled eggs, they slow down the coagulation of protein curds and keep them creamy and rich. By opting for a quick spray of canola oil instead, you can achieve a wildly different texture, allowing those proteins to join together for something a bit more solid and with a slight chew. Griddles also allow maximum surface area contact with direct heat, helping them cook quickly without burning them or making them tough. This is partially why breaking out the griddle is great when making breakfast for a crowd, and you can always add other foods like pancakes and bacon while you prepare the eggs.

Since you won't be able to rely on fat for texture, it's also important to use Cracker Barrel's preferred griddle temperature of 225 degrees Fahrenheit. This is closer to a medium heat, which keeps the eggs fluffy but still not quite creamy. The restaurant also employs one expert tip for quality scrambled eggs: using farm-fresh ingredients. These have a richer flavor to compensate for less fat and firmer whites to help keep the fluffy shape while you eat them.

When a breakfast item is so good but also so simple, a lot of its quality boils down to technique. Cooking with less fat gives you a smaller margin of error, and a griddle can take some getting used to, so keep your eggs in constant motion and don't be afraid to lean on a bit of added water to level up your breakfast.

When you cook scrambled eggs in a small pan, even a small amount will quickly drop its temperature. The same isn't necessarily true for a griddle, especially if you use one with a heavy-duty steel cooktop that retains a ton of heat, but it also responds quickly when the flame is lowered, allowing precise control of temperature throughout cooking. Using two spatulas to continuously move and fold your eggs is a great way to help them cook evenly. Plus, the successive folded layers only build on all that fluffiness and make them fantastic as an ingredient in things like a breakfast sandwich or burrito.

When it comes to keeping eggs fluffy, but not too rich or runny, your best bet is a simple splash of water. Added moisture, but no fat, steams the curds a bit, helping them plump up without growing dense. While too much will make them soupy and flavorless, a tablespoon per three eggs does a great job. The added moisture also helps prevent them from drying out when using something as hot and fast as a large surface area griddle, so it can be a great tool if you've never cooked on a flat-top before.

#9786. Citations vs Promotional Links: 3 Tests to Spot the Difference

The Green Standard Editing Protocol for Internet Publishing.

The Green Standard Editing Protocol for Internet Publishing.

The Green Standard Editing Protocol for Internet Publishing.

When fleshing out an article, it’s often necessary to include citations and links to other sources. It’s important for SEO, but it’s also important to show the readers that your claims aren’t being pulled from thin air. However, it’s easy to fall into the trap of including promotional links that bring down the credibility of your article.

If you’re confused about how to differentiate between legitimate citations and promotional links, don’t worry; HackerNoon has you covered. Here are 3 tests to get to the bottom of the truth.

Look at the link and where it’s at. If it’s attached to generic text that absolutely needs no backlink, it’s a promotional link. Generic text, in this context, means keyword phrases that are just stuffed into the article for SEO purposes.

When deciding which is the best cloud platform to choose, developers usually look for these features.

“Best cloud platform to choose” needs no backlink, and it’s clear that it’s just there to promote a specific cloud platform. Promotional link for sure.

However, if the link is backing up and is attached to a specific claim, then it’s a bona fide citation. Here’s an example:

According to RealNews.com, 96% of people like to make up statistics on the fly.

It makes sense for the link to be there because you want to cite the place where you got the info from, which, in this case, is RealNews.com.

Think about your source. Was it really necessary for you to pick that one? What happens if you swapped it with a different source? Do things remain the same, or does that drastically change things?

According to SEOLinkStuffing.com, water has a slight blue tint to it

Water is blue is such a generic piece of info that you could’ve used any neutral source. The only reason to use SEOLinkStuffing.com as the source would be to send traffic its way; therefore, it can be considered a promotional link.

Here’s an example of swapping it with a neutral source instead:

According to the U.S. Geological Survey, water has a slight blue tint to it.

Same exact claim, but having a neutral source adds more weight to the point you’re trying to make, and it makes your article appear more legitimate.

When people click on the link that you put in your article, what will they see? Will they see legitimate info? Or will they be bombarded in the face with promotional content trying to sell them something?

You click on the link and immediately get hit with “Book a Demo!”, and you have a ton of branding and marketing for a specific company or tool.

This is not a good look. If people feel as if you wanted them to click on the link just to sell them something, your credibility is instantly destroyed.

You click on the link, and the only thing the destination website wishes to give you is information. No overly promotional stuff. No Pricing or Services tab in the header.

This is what you want out of a citation. Its only purpose is to back up one of your claims, not to sell you a product.

Use these three tests to figure out whether you’re adding real sources or promotional links to your article and watch your credibility fly through the roof.

#9780. The Canadian Bacon In A McDonald's Egg McMuffin Isn't Slow-Brined

Along with the fact that the McDonald's Egg McMuffin is endlessly customizable (even the simple addition of extra butter upgrades the sandwich), its base ingredients make for a bite that is a symphony of rich, savory flavors and includes enough variety of textures to keep your mouth interested until the very end. One of the most compelling components of the once good, now great McMuffin is the Canadian bacon: the thin, disc-shaped meat that seemingly has more in common with ham than the crispy strips we associate with bacon. It might interest you to know that this tender slab of pork doesn't get its salty flavor from a slow brine, or really, any immersive procedure at all. Instead, the brine is actually injected into the meat during the manufacturing process, according to Food Tech Today (per YouTube).

McDonald's hasn't publicly released which of its partners actually produces its Canadian bacon, but it's as good a guess as any that it could be Lopez Foods, a long-time known beef supplier for the burger chain. Whoever manufactures the Canadian bacon, though, does so by following a highly mechanized process, where the pork loins, fresh from the slaughterhouse, go through a series of machines in the plant. One of these machines contains hundreds of needles that automatically inject the brine, made mostly of salt, sugar, sodium nitrate, and food coloring, into the trimmed but still largely unprocessed pork as it travels down the production line. The brine is necessary for flavor, as well as texture, to ensure the meat stays tender and juicy.

The journey those pork loins make from the moment they enter the processing plant until they end up as slices on a McDonald's McMuffin is actually fascinating, and no part is more interesting than the second half of the operation. This is where the pork is packed tightly into sleeves, steamed for around five hours until fully cooked, and the brine has the opportunity to permeate and distribute all throughout the meat. Then, the tubes of pork are sliced into exact discs by a machine and placed in its vacuum-sealed packaging. Instead of arriving frozen at McDonald's locations, as the sausage does, the Canadian bacon arrives merely refrigerated.

To cook the Canadian bacon and give it the requisite browning that appears on the finished McMuffin, employees simply grab a number of the slices and place them down in the front of the clamshell grills, so that they're not under the lid. They cook for eight seconds on each side, and unlike McDonald's burgers, which don't get flipped, an employee must manually turn them over. The precise timing allows the slices to warm through, but not cook for so long that they crisp up, which could then be a hop, skip, and a jump away from burning and wasting Canadian bacon.

#9778. Top 10 AI Tools in 2023 That Will Make Your Life Easier

In this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries. These tools are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The tools included in our list are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for a variety of applications. Some of the tools focus on natural language processing, such as ChatGPT and Grammarly, while others focus on image and video generation, such as DALL-E and Lumen5. This list is a great starting point for anyone looking to explore the possibilities of AI and how it can be applied to their business or project.

#9775. Former McDonald's Chef Reveals Why Fast Food Chicken Tenders Are Smaller Than They Look

From accusations of serving heavily processed food to concerns about the temperature of scalding coffee, fast food chains have faced their fair share of backlash over the years. One thing they could usually fall back on was offering an affordable meal, but with soaring prices, that promise is becoming harder to keep. And while customers have certainly felt the rising costs, they've not noticed a corresponding increase in quality. In fact, some are beginning to question whether they're really getting any bang for their buck at all.

Enter shrinkflation, the increasingly common practice of charging more while quietly reducing portion sizes. Even more frustratingly, some chains might be selling you a product that looks perfectly generous on the outside but contains surprisingly little actual meat. In a documentary produced by More Perfect Union, former McDonald's corporate chef Mike Haracz revealed some industry tricks fast food chains use to make their chicken tenders look bigger than they actually are. Right off the bat, Haracz explained why some chains compromise on product quality in the first place. "They are willing to serve not as good of a product because they can make more money and serve more people," he shared. "Make it as cheap as possible, so they can get the most profit."

So how exactly do they pull it off? According to Haracz, there's more than one way to make a chicken tender like bigger without actually adding more chicken. One approach involves the marinade. By injecting or soaking the meat in a saltwater brine, manufacturers can increase its moisture content and weight, making the tender appear plumper. Then there's the breading. Using a thicker coating, double-dredging the chicken, or opting for bulkier panko breadcrumbs can all add extra volume to the finished product.

It's no secret that nobody likes shrinkflation. Just look at the brutal way those accused of it were treated in the Middle Ages. These days, however, mob justice has largely been replaced by people venting their frustrations on Reddit. Reacting to the More Perfect Union video, one Redditor wrote, "Any company that is publicly traded has a fiduciary duty to sell you the worst possible product for the most money possible. Fast food is no exception." This user might be onto something since chicken tenders aren't the only fast food product that has been accused of shrinkflation.

According to Fox News, chicken is the number one best-selling fast food protein on DoorDash, with beef burgers not far behind. While anything labeled 100% ground beef legally cannot contain added water, and coating it in extra breading is obviously out of the question, that doesn't mean chains are short on other tricks to cut costs and make their beef go further. According to the More Perfect Union documentary, one common approach is to use beef with a lower lean-to-fat ratio, which is typically cheaper than leaner blends. However, the price trade-off becomes apparent once the patty hits the grill.

As the fat renders out during cooking, the burger can shrink considerably, leaving you with a smaller finished patty than you might expect from its raw weight — and it's the raw weight that most fast food joints use in advertising. Another trick involves the toppings themselves. By reducing the size of ingredients like lettuce, tomatoes, pickles, and even the bun, restaurants can make them more proportionate to a smaller patty, helping maintain the illusion of a generously filled burger even when there's less meat underneath.

#9774. 16 pumpkin recipes, from cakes and cookies to bars and bread: We've got a marbled pumpkin cake, chewy pumpkin cookies, and even pumpkin milk bread.

It’s that time of year when pumpkin spice everything starts appearing on store shelves — candles, lip balm, air fresheners, beer, and of course, the ubiquitous PSL (pumpkin spice latte). That means fall is here, and more importantly, that pumpkin should make a grand return to your kitchen! Pull out your canned pumpkin — or better yet, make your own pumpkin purée — and stock your pantry with pumpkin pie spice, because we have the best pumpkin recipes to bake this fall.

This Pumpkin Swirl Cake takes my breath away every time I unmold it from its intricate loaf pan. The anticipation keeps building until I slice into the pound cake-like loaf and reveal the swirled pattern inside, marbled with both vanilla and spiced pumpkin batter. (Don’t fret if you don’t have the specialty loaf pan — this can also be baked in a standard loaf pan and adorned with a simple confectioners’ sugar icing.)

To make this recipe, you'll need: Patch O Pumpkins Loaf Pan and Pure Vanilla Plus

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice and Sparkling Sugar

A cousin of Belgian-style Liège waffles, these Pumpkin Sugar Crunch Waffles have caramelized edges and a pleasant chew that’s reminiscent of brioche. The yeasted batter has pumpkin in it for flavor and color, plus Swedish pearl sugar that melts into pockets of crispy sugar. The best part? The batter rests overnight, so if you prepare it the night ahead, all you have to do the next morning is scoop and cook the batter for hot, crispy waffles in just a few minutes.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Sugar Crunch Waffles

To make this recipe, you'll need: Swedish Pearl Sugar

I used to make the same pumpkin pie recipe for years, and it always left me wanting a little more excitement. Then I found this Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie and never looked back! The generously spiced filling uses nutmeg, ginger, cloves, and Vietnamese cinnamon to create a more flavorful pie than traditional versions. The secret to its silky-smooth texture? Corn syrup, which is an invert sugar and keeps the custard from becoming grainy. Substitute another invert sugar like honey or maple syrup if you like; I use maple syrup.

Get the recipe: Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon, Ginger, and Nutmeg

Whenever I have these tender, golden scones on hand, I look forward to getting out of bed the next morning because I know they’re waiting for me. They can be easily customized to use a range of mix-ins, depending on what you have in your pantry. My personal preference is a mix of crystallized ginger and Cinnamon Sweet Bits.

Get the recipe: Harvest Pumpkin Scones (or Gluten-Free Pumpkin Scones)

To make this recipe, you'll need: Mini Diced Ginger and Cinnamon Sweet Bits

If you’re looking for a way to make your whole kitchen smell like fall, these one-bowl, easy pumpkin muffins deliver — and fast. They’re ready in under an hour, so you can spend less time measuring, mixing, and cleaning and more time tackling your autumn bucket list.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Standard Muffin Pan

Making banana bread is an almost weekly activity in my house — except during fall, when we pivot to pumpkin bread instead. This is a quick, easy bake that satisfies my craving for something pumpkin-y, and it uses a simple trick to concentrate the pumpkin flavor and ensure the loaf is perfectly textured: The pumpkin purée is reduced on the stovetop to cook off excess moisture. (The process is similar to browning butter.) As a result, the final loaf is packed with pumpkin flavor.

Get the recipe: The Most Pumpkin Pumpkin Chocolate Chip Bread

To make this recipe, you'll need: Ginger and Semisweet Chocolate Chips

These bars have all the cozy, spiced goodness of the classic dessert in a portable, crowd-friendly form. The buttery, brown sugar crust gets pressed into the pan (no rolling out pie dough!), and the silky pumpkin filling comes together with just a handful of ingredients. The (optional but highly recommended) sour cream whipped topping brings a slight tanginess and completes the traditional pumpkin pie experience.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This Pumpkin Milk Bread is exceptionally soft, squishy, and feather-light, while also packing in a lot of pumpkin. Pumpkin can often weigh down baked goods, but here the combination of a tangzhong, bread flour, and a long mix makes this bread simultaneously moist and high-rising.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant Yeast

This tender pumpkin crumb cake is for people who double the chocolate chips in pumpkin bread and the streusel on coffee cake. Atop the thin layer of spiced pumpkin cake lays a heavy blanket of buttery crumbs with a bold chocolate flavor, thanks to Dutch-processed cocoa powder.

Get the recipe: Chocolate-Pumpkin Crumb Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Black Cocoa

These Pumpkin Cupcakes, with their piped swirl of cream cheese frosting, are the ideal way to celebrate fall birthdays. The cupcakes are super tender, thanks to the addition of cake flour and oil. Sour cream and brown sugar add tanginess and molasses-y sweetness while also preventing the cupcakes from being dry.

My husband’s favorite fall dessert is Pumpkin Whoopie Pies, hands down. He can’t resist these subtly sweet cakes sandwiching rich cream cheese filling. This recipe has a few extra bells and whistles to take it over the top: Bread and Cake Enhancer to keep the cakes extra soft and fresh, xanthan gum in the filling to give it a smooth mouthfeel, and diced crystallized ginger for a bit of extra zing in the filling.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Bread and Cake Enhancer, Xanthan Gum, and Mini Diced Ginger

The next time there’s a rainy weekend, I’m taking on a project bake: our Pumpkin Cream Cheese Danish. It’s a multiday process and laminating dough is a labor of love, but the final product is worth the effort: buttery, crisp pastries filled with pumpkin and sweet cream cheese.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Cream Cheese Danish

To make this recipe, you'll need: Baker’s Special Dry Milk

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This Pumpkin Layer Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting is a show-stopping dessert featuring spiced layers of cake, not-too-sweet cream cheese frosting, and a blanket of melted caramel poured over the top. Will it be slightly messy to serve? Yes. Will anyone mind? Absolutely not.

It has two layers of espresso swirl tucked within a moist, spiced cake. Make it in your favorite Bundt pan or serve it as a loaf if you’re more of simple-is-better person. #9769. Review: Starbucks' 2026 Holiday Menu Features Sugar, Spice, And One Drink That's Not-So-Nice

Spooky season has come to a close, which means our favorite chains are moving on to their next seasonal menus, and Starbucks is joining in on the action. The coffee giant has officially swapped out pumpkin for gingerbread, rolling out its highly anticipated holiday menu with a whopping six new drinks. That's a far cry from last year's holiday launch, which featured just one addition to the chain's nationwide drink lineup: the Eggnog Latte, returning after a four-year hiatus.

With eight items joining the lineup this year, deciding which ones are worth a try to ring in the holiday season can be a challenge. Luckily, we've done the taste testing for you. From festive drinks to savory bites, we're breaking down which of Starbucks' newest holiday offerings deserve a spot on your nice list and which ones may belong on the naughty list instead. Here's everything you need to know about Starbucks' new holiday menu items.

To conduct my taste test, I ordered each new menu item with no customizations. I made sure to try each drink at my local Starbucks location to avoid any watering down, melting, or cooling off. As for the food items, especially the Grilled Cheese, I tried to sample them as quickly as possible to enjoy them at their highest quality.

As Food Republic's resident Starbucks taste tester, I've tried everything from the chain's limited-time Peanuts Drinks from fall 2026 to last year's Target-exclusive Frozen Peppermint Hot Chocolate. In doing so, I've gained a good understanding of what can make or break a Starbucks drink, allowing me to come into my taste test prepared to conduct a thorough, honest review of the new launch.

The most important factors I considered during my taste test were flavor, presentation, and innovation. A drink was most successful when it possessed a bold yet balanced flavor that matched its description, looked as good as it tasted, and felt like it added something new to Starbucks' current menu offerings.

Now, I've certainly never whipped up a perfect tiramisu and usually prefer to keep my coffee and my dessert separate. But based on the few times I have enjoyed the classic dessert, I felt this was a pretty good representation of it. The drink had a rich, creamy texture, with a sweetness that was present but not overwhelming. The vanilla and espresso flavors complemented one another beautifully, while the mascarpone cold foam added an extra layer of creaminess that brought it all together.

Is tiramisu to be a holiday dessert? That's up for debate, but its rich notes and flavors fit right in with Starbucks' other seasonal offerings. In fact, this drink was so tasty it just so happened to be my favorite of the bunch, something I certainly wasn't expecting. Considering the latte is available both hot and iced, I'd be curious to see how the iced version compares to its warmer counterpart.

Now, I typically don't usually go for cold brew at Starbucks. As a certified sweet coffee lover, they typically turn out to be a bit too on the bitter side for me. But this drink was actually super flavorful for a cold brew. The notes of chocolate and vanilla syrup gave the drink a bit of a sweetness to mask that usual slight cold brew bitterness. As the mascarpone cold foam gradually melted into the drink, I found myself liking it even more as it added a sweetness and creaminess to it. And as far as presentation goes, it's certainly a looker — and not only because of the super cute new holiday cup design.

If you're already a fan of Starbucks' cold brew, consider this a fun, sweet swap when you're in the mood for a treat. And if you don't typically tend to enjoy the drink, this might be the perfect opportunity to give it another shot.

It's safe to say many Starbucks fans were not happy when the Apple Crisp drink lineup did not make a comeback for fall 2026. But it seems that Starbucks is trying to bring back the apple flavor this winter in the form of a Refresher instead of a shaken espresso or macchiato.

I never got to try Starbucks' Apple Crisp drinks, so I'm note sure this new colorful Refresher lineup will scratch the same itch for Apple Crisp fans. But with that said, I thought this drink was really successful. Refreshers can be finicky; I've had many that just didn't meet the mark and felt like an attempt in some kind of secret Starbucks mission to make a Refresher in every color of the rainbow. Thankfully, that wasn't the case here.

The Apple Pomegranate Lemonade Refresher was actually quite tasty. The lemonade and apple flavors merge together to almost create this sour apple, green jolly rancher kind of effect. It's bright and refreshing, which certainly isn't the classic holiday flavor profile, but I think it's a useful addition to Starbucks' menu (sometimes you just don't want a rich, warm-spiced beverage).

Plus, it had one of the best — if not the best — presentations of the day. The green and red colors came together to form a beautifully festive drink. If I had to give one critique, the pomegranate pearls were surprisingly difficult to pop this time around. Otherwise, I didn't have many complaints about this new beverage. It's fun, and while it may not taste like Christmas in a cup, it sure looks the part.

Next in my taste test was the Snowy Apple Pomegranate Refresher. If you're unfamiliar with Starbucks' Refresher lineup, the drinks are typically available with one of three bases: water, lemonade, or coconut milk. The coconut milk versions typically have fun name variations and this one certainly didn't disappoint in that department.

Overall, the drink was enjoyable but not really a standout for me. While I've typically preferred coconut milk Refreshers over their lemonade counterparts I felt as though the opposite was true for this particular flavor.

Usually, coconut milk seems to make for a more complementary base because it allows the Refresher flavors to shine without getting overpowered by the tartness of lemonade. But apple and coconut milk aren't necessarily a natural flavor match. While they didn't clash in this drink, they also didn't complement each other as well as the apple and lemonade flavors did. Still, the drink was sweet, with a subtle apple flavor, and a festive, Christmas-inspired appearance. If coconut milk is your Refresher base of choice, I certainly think you'd enjoy this new addition.

This next drink was so good that it ended up being my second favorite of the bunch (though a very close second to the Tiramisu Velvet Latte). The Iced Caramel Brulée Cream Chai (which also comes in a hot version if that's your chai of choice) consists of Starbucks' classic chai with a caramel brulée sauce, topped with Caramel Brulée Cold Foam and caramel brulée bits. If that description tells you anything, it's that Starbucks really isn't short-changing customers when it comes to the caramel brulée in this drink. And it works.

Now that I think about it, it's wild to me that this combo didn't exist earlier. Caramel brulée and chai seem to be a match made in flavor heaven. Chai already brings such a warm, cozy flavor profile to any drink, and the addition of caramel brulée gave it a toasty, buttery, yet sweet finish. As a chai lover, I can say with confidence that the Iced Caramel Brulée Cream Chai is a beverage I'll likely reorder this holiday season.

To me, it's an odd choice on Starbucks' part. Out of all of the holiday flavors to pair with matcha, why choose one that's so subtle? This drink pretty much just tasted like a regular matcha with sprinkles on it. And when a classic matcha is almost a dollar less at $5.45 (for a Grande, at least), cold foam and sprinkles just don't seem like enough to justify the upcharge. If you're a die-hard matcha fan and are looking to ever-so-subtly get into the holiday spirit, I suppose this could be a worthy choice. But in any other scenario, I'd pretty strongly advise against this one.

This might shock you, but I've never had a grilled cheese sandwich before today. Seriously. I'm not anti-cheese or anything, but it's just not a dish I ever felt that inclined to try. And boy, can I tell you, this was certainly quite the grilled for a first experience.

First, the sandwich is incredibly rich. With three types of cheese (cheddar, parmesan, and mozzarella), Dijon mustard, caramelized onion jam, and, of course, braised short rib, it's certainly decadent — and a tasty bite at that

The cheese is thick and rich (though not as melted as I had hoped, likely due to the time spent photographing each item before trying them — so definitely enjoy this one while it's hot), and the caramelized onion jam adds an unexpected touch of sweetness. The braised short rib is salty, adds a nice textural element, and makes the sandwich a bit more filling than it otherwise would be.

Given how rich this sandwich is, it's probably not the kind of thing you may want to start your day with if you prefer a lighter breakfast. (I certainly won't be ordering it at 8:30 a.m. again.) But that aside, it was a solid addition to Starbucks' new offerings, serving as a more elevated version of the chain's classic grilled cheese. A true grilled cheese fan may have a better frame of reference for whether this sandwich has a bit too much going on. But for my part, it was a pretty solid sandwich.

Finally, we've got the Bearista Cake Pop to wrap things up. Starbucks describes it as a cake pop inspired by its mega-viral Starbucks Bearista Glass Cold Cup, which sent the Internet into a frenzy last winter. Overall, the cake pop was good — I mean, it would be pretty hard to mess up a cake pop.

Still, there were some notable differences in flavor and texture compared to the chain's other cake pops. First and foremost, this cake pop is a great pick if you're a milk chocolate fan. I've found that some of Starbucks' other chocolate-coated cake pops, like the Hedgehog, have a darker chocolate coating to them. This one leans more milk chocolate though, which I personally appreciated.

Though I did miss the added textural element of the white morsel sprinkles found on the Birthday Cake Pop, the cute bear design made up for it. After all, a lot of the fun of Starbucks' cake pops usually comes from gobbling up the adorable new designs. And this one certainly wins in the cuteness factor (and thankfully, unlike its namesake, won't have you standing in a long line outside of Starbucks at 5 a.m. to snag it).

Still, the disappointment of the chain's new matcha offering doesn't take away from what I believe to be the success of pretty much every other item. Three drinks in particular really stood out to me: the Tiramisu Velvet Latte, Iced Caramel Brulée Cream Chai, and Apple Pomegranate Lemonade Refresher. All three beverages did an excellent job of pairing flavors that naturally complement each other; they all felt aligned with the holiday season in one way or another (whether through flavors or appearance) and offered something genuinely exciting to Starbucks' current menu that I could see myself ordering again.

After last year's relatively limited holiday launch, it's refreshing to see Starbucks take a few more chances with its seasonal offerings in 2026. And while not every item was a blue-ribbon winner, the chain delivered a well-rounded lineup of new drinks that feel worth getting excited about. Whether they have the staying power to become new holiday staples remains to be seen, but for now, I'd say Starbucks has given us plenty of reasons to celebrate.

Starbucks' new holiday menu items launched on November 5 and will be available for a limited time. Prices for the Grande size of the new drinks range from $5.45 to $6.75 (though prices may vary by location).

As for the new food items, the Bearista Cake Pop is priced at $3.45, while the Braised Short Rib Grilled Cheese is priced at $7.95, making it the most expensive of the new holiday menu items and a bit pricier than the chain's regular Crispy Grilled Cheese sandwich, which costs $7.25.

While any of Starbucks' new menu items can be a part of a healthy diet in moderation, if you're looking for the specifics on the nutritional information of the new additions, we've got you covered. The Apple Pomegranate Refresher beverages are the lightest of Starbucks' new holiday menu items. The Snowy Apple Drink contains 130 calories, with 26 grams of carbs, 0 grams of protein, and 2.5 grams of fat for a Grande size. Meanwhile, the Apple Pomegranate Lemonade Refresher contains 140 calories, with 33 grams of carbs, 0 grams of protein, and 0 grams of fat.

The Iced Caramel Brulée Cream Chai is among the more decadent of the new offerings as it contains 400 calories, with 61 grams of carbs, 8 grams of protein, and 14 grams of fat. Meanwhile, the most decadent new drink is the Tiramisu Velvet Latte. The beverage contains 460 calories, with 65 grams of carbs, 11 grams of protein, and 19 grams of fat.

In terms of the food items, the Bearista Cake Pop is a relatively light sweet treat, containing 160 calories with 20 grams of carbs, 2 grams of protein, and 8 grams of fat. The Braised Short Rib Grilled Cheese is the most decadent of the new holiday menu items as it contains 640 calories, with 56 grams of carbs, 26 grams of protein, and 35 grams of fat.
